catalogTitle: סעודת פורים: Purim Seudah Zeidins Cholem

oneLiner.en: At the Purim seudah the Mashgiach teaches that on Purim the holiness of the Kodesh HaKodashim and of Yom Kippur comes down to every Jew, and that the gates of mercy open to whoever knocks.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the kavanos of each day's tefillah and explains that Purim and Shushan Purim are the days of Esther and Mordechai, in which Hashem alone will build Yerushalayim. Purim is like Yom Kippur, but on Purim the holiness comes to the Jew: only the Kohen Gadol entered the Kodesh HaKodashim, and Parvah gave his life merely to see him, while on Purim the Kodesh HaKodashim comes to everyone. He goes on to Esther's thirty days, the Egyptian and Yisro, Daniel and Haman, Shaul's failure against Amalek and Mordechai's repair, the gates of mercy that open to one who knocks, Mordechai's kometz against Haman's silver, Haman's downfall, and Yisro and the latecomers for whom the Megillah was given. After a long song about a grandfather's dream of Moshiach and the Ani Maamin, he closes with Shushan Purim and Yerushalayim.

en: Each day's tefillah opens something different; Purim and Shushan Purim are the days of Esther and Mordechai, and in such days Hashem alone will build Yerushalayim, beyond our own deeds.
Purim is like Yom Kippur, the Kodesh HaKodashim of time, but on Purim one does not go to Yom Kippur; Yom Kippur comes to the Jew.
No one was ever allowed to see the Kohen Gadol inside the Kodesh HaKodashim, yet on Purim the Kodesh HaKodashim comes to every Jew, and drinking until 'lo yada' is meant to reach that level.
Mordechai 'ben Kish' knocked on the gates of mercy and they opened; every Purim is the same Purim, and the gates open to whoever knocks.
Shaul, of Binyamin, could not wipe out Amalek; Mordechai, 'ish Yehudi' and 'ish Yemini', repaired it.
Amalek attacks the stragglers who come late, and Hashem fights for them; the whole of Purim and the Megillah were given for the latecomers.
Shushan Purim was made in honor of Yerushalayim; every Jew is bound up with Yerushalayim, and one who thinks of Yerushalayim on Purim is there.

candidateTopics: Kohen Gadol in the Kodesh HaKodashim

title.en: The days of Esther and Mordechai

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that every day's tefillah has its own kavanos, that Purim and Shushan Purim are the days of Esther and Mordechai, and that Yerushalayim will be built 'b'karov', by these neighboring days, by Hashem alone.

He brings that Yom Kippur is 'ke-Purim' and that Yom Kippur is the Kodesh HaKodashim of time. As the place of the Mikdash went along with the Jews in the desert, so on Purim Yom Kippur and its teshuvah come to the Jew.

He tells of Parvah, who dug a tunnel to see the Kohen Gadol enter the Kodesh HaKodashim, and asks why a chamber was named after him. His mesirus nefesh to see the Kohen Gadol's radiant form was itself an achievement; on Purim the Kodesh HaKodashim comes to every Jew, and that is why one drinks.

He asks why Esther says she has not been called to the king 'these thirty days'. Thirty days is a full span of time in which a person can feel cut off; the Mashgiach says a Jew must not make such reckonings, and that now is a great eis ratzon.

He brings from the Arizal that the Egyptian whom Moshe killed and Yisro both carried the soul of Kayin, its bad side and its good side. By killing the Egyptian Moshe subdued Yisro's bad side, which is why Yisro's daughters said 'an Egyptian saved us'.

title.en: Daniel and Haman in one soul

summary.en: The Gemara identifies Memuchan with Haman while a Midrash identifies him with Daniel. The Mashgiach answers that, like the Egyptian and Yisro, Daniel and Haman share one soul, so both are true.

He asks why Shaul did not wipe out Amalek, though Binyamin is the right side against Amalek's left. As Shimshon fell through a woman and could not be Moshiach, Shaul failed through his mother's side; Mordechai, whose lineage joins Yehuda and Binyamin, repaired it.
A niggun.

title.en: Ben Kish: knocking on the gates of mercy

summary.en: He brings the Gemara's reading of Mordechai's lineage: Yair, Shimi and Kish, who knocked on the gates of mercy and they opened. Where is the opening hinted? Hashem is merciful, and when one knocks it is surely opened. Every Purim is the same Purim, and the gates open to whoever knocks. After a pause he adds that everything comes from the Torah, so the wonders of Purim required a Megillah.

He brings the Gemara in which Haman found Mordechai teaching the laws of kemitzah. Haman complained that Jews eat and drink; the laws of kemitzah, where flour may slip between thin fingers, show that a Jew may need to be fat. He adds a hint: a Jewish kamtzan's small gift is greater than a gentile's largest, since Hashem sees the inner thought, and so the kometz pushed away Haman's ten thousand.
On 'vachamas hamelech shachachah' he brings the Midrash that the king's anger subsided twice, once for Esther and once for Vashti, whom Haman had advised to kill.

title.en: Haman and the rasha who asked for warm plums

summary.en: He asks why Haman, second to the king, still provoked a quarrel with Mordechai, and answers with a story the Ba'al Shem Tov laughed over: a wicked man demanded warm plums because he wanted to know where he stood, and his punishment began with that and went back to everything else. So too Haman's downfall began with Esther and went back to Vashti.

title.en: The Purim seudah and 'ad d'lo yada'

summary.en: He connects the Purim seudah with Purim being like Yom Kippur, and brings the Arizal on saying 'baruch' while one no longer knows the difference, adding a thought of his own.

title.en: Hashem's name in 'Yavo hamelech v'Haman hayom'

summary.en: He brings that the first letters of 'Yavo hamelech v'Haman hayom' form Hashem's name and that the last letters stand reversed. Purim must bring light into all the worlds and daas into kedushah; even the commotion of Purim brings down blessing, and now is a great eis ratzon.

Yisro heard of the splitting of the sea and the war with Amalek. Amalek attacked the stragglers, and Hashem made a special war for those who come late; seeing this, Yisro the latecomer came, and for him the Torah was given again. For the late generations Hashem gave the Megillah, a new Torah, and the whole of Purim was made for those who lack zrizus.

The Mashgiach speaks of saying rhymes on Purim: as at a wedding, a rhyme is a yichud, and Purim is a great wedding. He brings the Midrash of the lion's feast at which the fox sang, and speaks of the Hamans of every generation.
A long song about a grandfather's dream of the coming of Moshiach.

title.en: Mesirus nefesh and the Ani Maamin

summary.en: After a lively interlude, the Mashgiach says that now, at the end of the year, is the moment to accept emunah with true mesirus nefesh, bringing the Ba'al Shem Tov's teaching about rolling down a mountain for Hashem. The Ani Maamin then begins with a Yiddish rendering.
The Ani Maamin is sung with a Yiddish rendering.
At the end of the year a Jew makes a reckoning and thanks Hashem for every Yom Tov of the year. He then asks, in Purim style, where each Yom Tov is found in the Megillah.

Shushan Purim was made in honor of Yerushalayim, and 'asher hoglah mi-Yerushalayim' teaches that every Jew is bound up with Yerushalayim. Where a person's thought is, there he is; on Purim one who thinks of Yerushalayim is there, and from there one can rise higher. He closes asking Hashem where His honor is, and with the gifts that will be brought to Moshiach.

oneLiner.en: At the Purim seudah the Mashgiach explains that the light of Purim comes from a place above reason that can be revealed only through hiddenness, and he ends with the Ani Maamin and a tefilah for the redemption.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by asking why the Purim seudah is held at night when it belongs by day, and answers that Purim is above reason, like the Gemara's 'achashtranim bnei haramachim' that no one understands. The Megillah, when spread out, sprays yeshuos through all the worlds. Amalek comes from Timna, meaning obstacles, and a Jew must not let them stop him. Jews quarrel because they possess truth and stubbornness, and tzedakah brings peace. Haman took a beam of fifty amos, the Name Yah, from Noach's ark, and was hanged on that very wood. Purim's light can be revealed only where Hashem is hidden: this is why His Name is absent from the Megillah and why Yerushalayim keeps only Shushan Purim. In the second part he speaks of the second decree and the fear of Mordechai, recites the Ani Maamin with explanation, and closes with techiyas hameisim and the redemption.

en: The seudah at night is above reason, like the 'achashtranim bnei haramachim' whose meaning the Gemara says is unknown.
When the Megillah is spread out, its letters spray yeshuos and lights through all the worlds.
Amalek comes from Timna, which tzaddikim read as obstacles, and a Jew must not let obstacles stop him.
Jews quarrel more than the nations because they possess truth and stubbornness, and giving tzedakah brings peace.
Haman's beam of fifty amos stood for the Name Yah, and he was hanged on the very wood he had prepared.
Purim's light can be revealed only where Hashem is hidden, so His Name is absent from the Megillah and Yerushalayim keeps only Shushan Purim.
Through the Ani Maamin the Mashgiach stresses that every Jew must believe with complete faith that Hashem alone guides everything.

title.en: Why the seudah is held at night

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the Purim seudah is held at night when it belongs by day, and answers that Purim is above reason, like the 'achashtranim bnei haramachim' no one understands. He reads 'kol haposhet yad' as spreading the Megillah, whose letters spray yeshuos, and explains that Purim is not bound by time.

The Mashgiach explains that Haman and Amalek come from Timna, which tzaddikim read as obstacles, and that a Jew must not let them stop him. He speaks of the inner point in every Jew, of the hidden 'kallah' quality of the Megillah, and of reaching 'ad delo yada'.

title.en: Machlokes among Jews and peace through tzedakah

summary.en: On the pesukim 'kol gevulech l'avnei chefetz' and 'rav shalom banayich', the Mashgiach brings the Netzach Yisrael: Jews quarrel because they have truth and stubbornness, and the more one learns the stronger it grows. The way to peace, he says, is tzedakah, which makes peace between the poor man and Hashem.
A niggun.

title.en: Haman's fifty-amah beam and the Name Yah

summary.en: The Mashgiach relates that Haman took a beam of fifty amos from Noach's ark, and shows by multiplication (hakaah) that fifty is the Name Yah, with which the war against Amalek is fought. Haman was hanged on the very wood 'asher heichin', and through this comes a great unity in all the worlds.

The Mashgiach notes that Shushan Purim is already beginning in Yerushalayim and speaks of Purim being revealed 'outside', in the weekdays. He asks Hashem that the light of Yerushalayim come out to the whole world.

title.en: Why Purim is revealed only in hiddenness

summary.en: Bringing the Kesav Sofer, the Mashgiach explains that Hashem's Name is absent from the Megillah because the miracle of Purim comes from so high a place that it can be revealed only where Hashem is hidden. Yerushalayim, with its revealed Shechinah, therefore cannot have Purim, only Shushan Purim, and people like us, he says, need the great yeshua of Purim itself.

title.en: Shushan on the Temple's eastern gate

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why Shushan, outside Eretz Yisrael, keeps Shushan Purim, and brings the Mishnah in Middos that Shushan was depicted on the eastern gate of the Beis HaMikdash. Against the view that this was for the Persian king's sake, he brings the Gemara on the name of Teverya, and concludes that in the future the light of Yerushalayim will spread out to the lowest places.
Another speaker.
The second part of the seudah opens with a niggun.

title.en: The second decree and the fear of Mordechai

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Haman's first letters could not be revoked, so a second decree was issued allowing the Jews to stand up for their lives without opposing the king's law. He notes that the Megillah says three times that the Jews did not touch the spoils, and that the miracle was the fear of Mordechai that fell on the officials.

title.en: The officials' fear and Haman's fall

summary.en: The Mashgiach returns to the fear of Mordechai that made the king's officials help the Jews, and speaks of Haman's downfall together with his sons.

title.en: Servants of Hashem, not of Achashverosh

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Arizal that the kedusha revealed all day on Purim is like that of Kesser, and speaks of sending mishloach manos to the Ribono shel Olam. He brings the Gemara that Hallel is not said on Purim because the Jews were still servants of Achashverosh, and says that now one must return to Hashem as His servants.
Interlude.

title.en: Yerushalayim and the Jews as servants of Hashem

summary.en: The Mashgiach speaks of the rebuilding of Yerushalayim and of the Jews as servants of Hashem rather than of a king, mentions Haman's offer of silver for the Jews, and says that a Jew who takes on himself to be Hashem's servant will come to Yerushalayim.
Interlude.

title.en: Ani Maamin: Hashem alone guides everything

summary.en: The Mashgiach says that the mesirus nefesh of the Jews brings out the simple faith every Jew has, and goes through the Ani Maamin: Hashem created and guides all creatures, no one can do good or harm without His will, He alone is One, one prays only to Him, and all the words of the prophets and the Sages of Israel are true.

title.en: Ani Maamin: Moshe Rabbeinu, the Torah and reward

summary.en: Continuing the Ani Maamin, the Mashgiach explains that Moshe Rabbeinu's prophecy is the root of all prophecy, that the whole Torah, Written and Oral, with all accepted seforim, goes back to Moshe, that it will not be exchanged, that Hashem knows every thought of man, and that He rewards every mitzvah.

The Mashgiach speaks of awaiting the redemption, perhaps already by Pesach, and of his belief that all the dried-out and lowly Jewish souls will come alive at techiyas hameisim. He closes with the wish that the remembrance be of the Ribono shel Olam rather than of Amalek.

oneLiner.en: At the Purim seudah the Mashgiach teaches that on Purim the hidden greatness of Mordechai and the eternal life of Klal Yisroel come out into the open, and that Purim, like Rosh Hashanah, builds the whole world.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with Haman's charge against the 'one nation, scattered and dispersed' and says that at the seudah the beauty and chein of the Jewish people must come out, with derech eretz. He explains why the Anshei Knesses haGedolah lowered Mordechai a level: his level of 'ad delo yada' was too hidden, and only so could it come out. He explains why Haman's rope tore and he broke his leg: Amalek is bound to Bilam, and the false netzach of Amalek fails before Netzach Yisroel. Through Moshe Rabbeinu's knowledge of the pulse he teaches that Klal Yisroel lives even when it seems lifeless. After singing about Jamale, he brings the Targum that 'ish Yehudi' is a man who thanks and davens, and that Esther stood in Yerushalayim in her thoughts. He explains the two laughs of an ehrliche Yid, ties Targum to tardeimah and to zivugim, calls Purim the building of the world, and closes with the Ani Maamin.

en: At the Purim seudah the beauty and chein of the Jewish people must come out, with great derech eretz; wild behavior that disturbs others or makes a chillul Hashem is not Purim.
Mordechai's level is 'ad delo yada', a hidden level that comes out only once a year; the Anshei Knesses haGedolah lowered him a level, and through this it went out into the open.
Purim is the day of netzach; Amalek, the kelipah of netzach, thought it would prevail, but its netzach is false and only Netzach Yisroel endures.
Klal Yisroel can look as if it has no sign of life, but one who knows the pulse sees that Jews live and will live.
A person is where his thoughts are: Esther, standing in Shushan, was in truth in Yerushalayim, and Jews in New York can live in Yerushalayim.
Purim is the bechinah of Targum and of tardeimah, and like Rosh Hashanah it is the building of the whole world.
According to the Targum, 'ish Yehudi' means a man who thanks Hashem and davens, and wherever Mordechai went or sat he was davening.

Haman and Amalek as the kelipah of netzach

title.en: Haman's charge and the beauty of Klal Yisroel

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens with Haman's charge that there is 'one nation, scattered and dispersed', and the Shechinah's answer: a people that accepts the kingship of Heaven in every land. At the Purim seudah, he says, Mordechai and Esther come down, and the beauty and chein of the Jewish people must come out, with derech eretz and without wildness.

title.en: Why Mordechai was lowered a level

summary.en: On 'Mordechai the Jew was second to the king, accepted by most of his brothers', the Mashgiach brings the Gemara that some of the Sanhedrin separated from him and that he was counted lower than before. He explains that Mordechai's level is 'ad delo yada', a hidden world, and asks why the Anshei Knesses haGedolah could lower Mordechai, when Heaven stopped them from counting Shlomo HaMelech among those without a share in the World to Come.

title.en: Mordechai's greatness goes out into the open

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that once the Anshei Knesses haGedolah lowered Mordechai a level, his level went out into the open, and he returns to the passuk of Mordechai as second to the king. He then turns to Haman and asks how Haman is connected to the lechem hapanim.

title.en: Haman's torn rope and broken leg

summary.en: The Mashgiach relates that when Haman was hanged the rope tore and he fell and broke his leg. Through the Zohar he shows that Amalek and Bilam share their letters, and since Bilam was lame Haman too had to be lamed. The rope tore because Purim is netzach: Amalek, the kelipah of netzach, thought it would prevail, but as Shmuel told Shaul, only Netzach Yisroel does not lie.

title.en: The eighth king and the pulse of Klal Yisroel

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the Torah does not write 'and he died' by Hadar, the last of the kings of Edom, while Divrei Hayamim does, and ties Hadar to the level of Moshiach. He brings a great mekubal, a talmid of the Arizal: Moshe Rabbeinu was expert in the pulse and Ezra was not, like a great doctor who feels a pulse in a patient others think is gone. So too Klal Yisroel may look lifeless, yet Netzach Yisroel does not lie: Jews live and will live.
Singing.

The Mashgiach asks the crowd for quiet and introduces his Jamale. He suggests that the name comes from Zalman, whose gematria is 127, like the 127 provinces, and reveals that every Jew is Jamale. He then begins a song about Jamale, a great gibbor and a rich man.
Singing.
Singing.
A song about Purim.

title.en: Ish Yehudi: a man who thanks and davens

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Targum that 'ish Yehudi' means a man who thanks Hashem and davens, and that wherever Mordechai walked or sat he was davening; on Purim this side of Mordechai is revealed. He tells how the Mogielnicer Rebbe began saying Nishmas and the Grodzisker hinted to the crowd to join, and asks the crowd to say Nishmas with him.
Singing.

The Mashgiach brings the Targum on 'she stood in the inner court of the king's house, opposite the king's house': Esther, with ruach hakodesh, davened facing the King in Yerushalayim. With the Ba'al Shem Tov's rule that a person is where his thoughts are, he explains why Shushan is tied to Yerushalayim, and says that Jews standing in New York can live in Yerushalayim.
Singing.

title.en: The two laughs and the month of laughter

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Lechovitcher's explanation of the two jesters in the Gemara who merited the World to Come: an ehrliche Yid needs two laughs, the world laughing at him and he laughing at the world, and he needs both. From Rashi on 'tzchok asah li Elokim' he explains that Adar, the month of laughter, draws down all the yeshuos.

The Mashgiach explains that Targum belongs to the lowest levels and is the bechinah of tardeimah, sleep, as in 'yeshno am echad', which is why the Megillah has so many Targumim. This explains the custom of going to Yonasan ben Uziel, who wrote the Targum, to daven for a shidduch: Adam HaRishon received his zivug through a tardeimah on Rosh Hashanah. With the Ba'al Shem Tov, everything a person needs is a zivug, and so Purim, like Rosh Hashanah, is the building of the whole world.
An interlude in the seudah.

The Mashgiach recites the Ani Maamin with a Yiddish rendering: Hashem is the Creator and is One, He has no body, only to Him one davens, the words of the nevi'im and the prophecy of Moshe Rabbeinu are true, the Torah will not be changed, He knows the thoughts of men, Moshiach will come, and the dead will live again.

catalogTitle: Serving Hashem with Joy; A Product of Appreciation (מזמור לתודה)

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that avodas Hashem rests on gratitude, which is why the morning prayers open with Mizmor Lesodah, and that true service must also be filled with joy.

abstract.en: Continuing Mizmor Lesodah, the Mashgiach teaches that a person who is not grateful to people will not be grateful to Hashem; ingratitude is animal-like, as shown by a bar mitzvah boy who complained about a hand-me-down suit. Gratitude lets a person see what Hashem does for him every moment, which is why Modim, Modeh Ani and Mizmor Lesodah come first, and on Shabbos we thank Hashem even for His hidden conduct of history. Adam HaRishon's first words to Hashem were ungrateful, while Bikurim, the first gift, declares that a Jew is not ungrateful. The Mashgiach reads from the will of a tzaddik who thanked Hashem for every small thing: a private room, a sharpened knife, glasses that did not break. Thanksgiving remains even in the future. Finally, Mizmor Lesodah calls for serving Hashem with joy: Ish stands for love, fear and joy, and a clear devar halacha before davening brings that joy.

en: The Mashgiach says avodas Hashem is built on thankfulness, and one who is not grateful to people will not be grateful to Hashem.
The first thing in prayer and in the day is thanks: Modeh Ani on waking, and Mizmor Lesodah right after Baruch She'amar.
One thanks Hashem both for the good one sees and for what one does not yet understand, believing that all is for the good of Klal Yisroel.
Through the will of a tzaddik, the Mashgiach shows how one can thank Hashem for every small and large thing, even something seemingly bad.
Avodas Hashem is incomplete without simcha; a mitzvah needs love, fear and joy.

candidateTopics: love, fear and joy in mitzvos

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens Mizmor Lesodah by teaching that a mensch must be grateful, that ingratitude to people leads to ingratitude to Hashem, and illustrates with a bar mitzvah boy who complained about his hand-me-down suit.
The Mashgiach explains Modim and why Mizmor Lesodah opens the psalms after Baruch She'amar; on Shabbos one thanks Hashem for His hidden conduct of history, and the day itself begins with Modeh Ani.

The Mashgiach contrasts Adam HaRishon, whose first conversation with Hashem showed ingratitude for his wife, with Bikurim, the first gift, through which a Jew declares he is not ungrateful; he ties this to the hundred daily brachos and the hundredth chapter of Tehillim.

The Mashgiach introduces a sefer by a tzaddik of about two hundred years ago, praised by the Rebbe of Lublin, explains when a pure person may write about himself, and begins reading how the tzaddik thanked Hashem for both good and bad, and for his private room.

The Mashgiach continues the tzaddik's will: he thanked Hashem for good news from his children, for what he could buy, for a sharpened knife, a remembered item, glasses that did not break and a found snuffbox; the Mashgiach then explains the two meanings of hodaah and that thanksgiving will remain even in the future.

From Mizmor Lesodah the Mashgiach teaches that avodas Hashem must be with simcha: the Levi'im's song supplied joy to a korban, Ish stands for love, fear and joy, and a clear devar halacha before davening brings the joy that tefillah needs.

oneLiner.en: At the Purim seudah the Mashgiach shows how the Jewish people survive only by miracle through their bond to the Torah, how Mordechai's prayer and Haman's admission reveal what truly belongs to Klal Yisroel, and how the holy wine of the Beis HaMikdash brought the Jews of Shushan to accept the Torah anew.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with Esther's fear that the Jews had transgressed the Ten Commandments, written 'from this side and that': every Jew has a letter in the Torah, and like the mem and samech of the Luchos, Jewish souls stand only by miracle, so they must stay bound to the Torah. He explains Mordechai ben Yair, ben Shimi and ben Kish, and says that today Mordechai knocks on the gates of mercy for us. From Haman's words 'all this is worth nothing to me' he draws the month of Tammuz and Mordechai's claim that whatever Esav holds belongs to Jerusalem. He then shows that the old wine at Achashverosh's feast was the sealed wine of the Beis HaMikdash, on which the Jews made Kiddush that Shabbos and came to accept the Torah anew. Later he speaks of matanos la'evyonim in the days of Moshiach, of Binyamin's silence and Rachel's signs, of Tamar, and of hoping for Moshiach despite every disappointment.

en: The Jewish people endure in exile only by miracle, and that miracle holds only as long as they stay bound to the Torah.
Mordechai's prayer brought light to the whole world, and on Purim in our time he knocks on the gates of mercy on our behalf.
Mordechai provoked Haman in order to arouse that whatever Esav and Tzor hold, including the month of Tammuz, truly belongs to Jerusalem and the Jews.
The Jews of Shushan made Kiddush that Shabbos on the sealed wine of the Beis HaMikdash, and through it they came to accept the Torah anew.
Rachel's silence passed to Binyamin, Shaul and Esther, and like Tamar, she would not bring the redemption at the price of shaming another Jew.

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens the seudah, recalls that Purim stands even higher than Shabbos, and says that the main seudah stretches into the night, when one can reach the true matters of Purim.

title.en: The Ten Commandments and the miracle of Jewish souls

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why Esther feared that the Jews had transgressed specifically the Ten Commandments, written 'from this side and that'. He explains that every Jew has a letter in the Torah, all the letters are included in the Ten Commandments, and like the mem and samech of the Luchos, Jewish souls stand only by miracle, so each Jew must bind himself to his letter.

title.en: Mordechai ben Yair, ben Shimi, ben Kish

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains Chazal on Mordechai's names: his prayer lit up the eyes of Israel, it was heard, and he knocked on the gates of mercy. He asks why Mordechai needed to knock, and answers that today Mordechai knocks for us; he then cries out that this is a fearful time and asks Hashem to bring Moshiach.

title.en: 'All this is worth nothing to me'

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Bnei Yissaschar that Haman's words 'all this is worth nothing to me' hold the name of Hashem for the month of Tammuz, and the Gemara that Haman's treasures were engraved on his heart. He brings the Chasam Sofer that whenever Haman boasted of his wealth, Mordechai reminded him that a slave's property belongs to his master, and asks why Mordechai provoked him.

The Mashgiach answers that Tzor was filled only from the ruin of Jerusalem, so whatever Esav holds belongs to the Jews; Mordechai wanted to arouse this in heaven, above all regarding the month of Tammuz that was given to Esav. Haman's admission and 'v'nahafoch hu' turn Tammuz over, and the name of Sivan, the month of Kabbolas HaTorah, extends into Adar.
An interlude in the seudah.

title.en: The holy wine at Achashverosh's feast

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains 'on the seventh day, when the king's heart was merry with wine' as the Shabbos of that feast, and asks how each guest could be given wine older than himself. He answers that Achashverosh took out the vessels of the Beis HaMikdash, among them sealed wine prepared for the nesachim; the Jews made Kiddush on it that Shabbos, which brought them to accept the Torah anew, and the 'guarded wine' is the gematria of Esther.
An interlude in the seudah.

title.en: Black like the bottom of a pot

summary.en: The Mashgiach calls on everyone to accept Torah learning with love, and explains why the Jews' darkness is compared to the bottom of a pot: the pot is black because something is cooking in it. So too now, in a very dark time before Moshiach, something great is cooking.

The Mashgiach speaks of the coming Shabbos: today is Purim, tomorrow Shushan Purim, the Purim of Yerushalayim, and then Shabbos; he asks what can still be added after Shushan Purim, and speaks of three days of Purim.
The Mashgiach speaks of Ohaliav ben Achisamach of the tribe of Dan, who worked together with Yehuda on the Mishkan, the lowliest together with the highest, and says that Hashem lifts up the fallen.

The Mashgiach takes up a question: when Moshiach comes and there are no poor, how will matanos la'evyonim be kept? He explains that Hashem wants no Jew to be an evyon, and answers with a great tzaddik who gave sweets to children, saying that children are the true evyonim.

The Mashgiach explains Binyamin's stone, yashfeh: he had a mouth and kept silent about the sale of Yosef. From Rachel's silence came Shaul, who did not tell of the kingship, and Esther, who did not reveal her people. He explains the hidden and revealed worlds of Leah and Rachel, and brings the Satmar Rav that a mouth that cannot keep silent when needed is not a mouth.

The Mashgiach explains that Yaakov wanted to unite the hidden and the revealed through Rachel, which would have been the light of Purim and of Moshiach, but Rachel gave her signs to Leah. Tamar did the same: she was ready to be burned rather than shame Yehuda, and Moshiach must not come at the cost of shaming a Jew.
An interlude in the seudah.
An interlude in the seudah.
An interlude in the seudah.
Purim songs at the seudah.
An interlude in the seudah.

The Mashgiach speaks of the hopes for Moshiach that ended in disappointment, from the time of Bar Koziba, whom Rabbi Akiva thought was Moshiach, and says that the hope of Klal Yisroel remains in place.

title.en: Pointing with the finger: 'we hoped for Him'

summary.en: The Mashgiach speaks of the dance Hashem will make for the tzaddikim, when each will point with his finger and say 'this is our G-d, we hoped for Him'. The hope of a Jewish heart after so many disappointments cannot be said with the mouth, only shown with the finger.

oneLiner.en: At the Purim seudah the Mashgiach explains how Purim, which came by lot and above understanding, repairs the sin of eating at Achashverosh's feast, draws sparks of holiness even out of Haman, and completes the 24th ornament of the kallah.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by explaining that Purim came through a lot, which is above understanding, and that Esther asked for an extra day in Shushan so the lot would be hers and not Haman's. He asks why the angels pleaded with tarshish, and answers that it is the stone of eating, tied to the Jews' enjoyment of Achashverosh's feast; the seudas Purim, the last of Purim's four mitzvos, corresponds to the last letter of Hashem's Name. He explains that Haman held a spark of holiness, since his descendants learned Torah in Bnei Brak, and that holiness reaches outward to retrieve such sparks, except on Pesach. He then asks how, according to Shmuel, the Megillah fits among the 24 holy books that parallel a kallah's 24 ornaments, and answers with the Bnei Yissaschar that on Purim it is a holy book. Finally he explains that Haman aimed his gallows at krias shema of the morning, and how the Tannaim in Bnei Brak repaired this.

en: All of Purim came through a lot, which is above understanding, and Esther asked for another day in Shushan so that the lot would be hers and not Haman's.
The angels' claim of tarshish rests on the Jews' enjoyment of Achashverosh's feast, since tarshish is the stone of eating; the seudas Purim answers it.
Haman held a spark of holiness, as his descendants learned Torah in Bnei Brak, and holiness reaches outward only to bring such sparks back in.

According to Shmuel the Megillah does not make the hands tamei, which raises the question of the 24 holy books that parallel a kallah's 24 ornaments; on Purim, the Mashgiach explains, the Megillah is a holy book and completes the 24th ornament.
Haman took wood from the Kodesh Hakodashim and wanted Mordechai hanged in the morning in order to stop his krias shema of shacharis.
The Tannaim who gathered in Bnei Brak repaired Haman's descendants there, so that they could say krias shema of the morning.

summary.en: Singing.
An interlude before the Mashgiach speaks.

title.en: Purim by lot, and Esther's extra day

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens with the words of tzaddikim that the main seudah is toward evening, when Purim begins in Yerushalayim. Since all of Purim came through a lot, which is above understanding, he explains that Esther asked for another day in Shushan so that the lot would be hers and not Haman's.

He brings the Gemara on the angels' claims before Hashem and asks what tarshish adds. Through Rabbeinu Bachya and the month of Shvat he shows it is the stone of eating, tied to the Jews' enjoyment of Achashverosh's feast, and explains that the seudas Purim, last of Purim's four mitzvos, corresponds to the last letter of Hashem's Name.
An interlude at the seudah.

title.en: Haman's spark of holiness and Bnei Brak

summary.en: The Mashgiach speaks of saying 'baruch Mordechai' and 'arur Haman', and explains that Haman held a spark of holiness, since his descendants learned Torah in Bnei Brak. From a sefer on Parshas Beshalach he explains that the foot of the last letter reaches outward, so every holy thing gives a little life outward in order to retrieve sparks, as the end of Shabbos reaches into the weekdays.

title.en: Pesach, and the Megillah's beginning and end

summary.en: He explains that Pesach is the exception, when holiness may not reach outward. He contrasts the Megillah's beginning of woe with its good ending, ties it to the Torah learned in Bnei Brak, and brings the Gemara that Esther asked the sages to write her for the generations. On Shushan Purim, he says, the holiness of Yerushalayim spreads over the land.
An interlude at the seudah, with l'chaim.

title.en: Is the Megillah among the 24 holy books?

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the dispute whether Megillas Esther makes the hands tamei, with Shmuel holding that it does not, and mentions Tosafos' question. He asks a stronger question: the 24 holy books parallel the 24 ornaments of a kallah, so according to Shmuel one ornament would be missing.

title.en: The ornaments above; the Megillah as a mitzvah object

summary.en: He answers that the ornaments always exist in Heaven and came down through the nevi'im, and that their completion awaits the days of Moshiach. He then brings the Bnei Yissaschar, who answers Tosafos that the Megillah is a mitzvah object like a shofar or a lulav, holy on Purim and not the whole year.

title.en: On Purim the kallah is fully adorned

summary.en: He explains the Bnei Yissaschar: on Purim the light of Moshiach is revealed, so on Purim the Megillah is one of the 24 holy books and the 24th ornament is completed. He brings the Kehillas Yaakov that 'kedas' alludes to the 24 ornaments, and reads Esther's request 'la'asos kedas hayom' in this light.

title.en: The Megillah's ornament, even in exile

summary.en: He counts which of the ornaments corresponds to Megillas Esther and connects it to Mordechai and Esther against Haman. He brings the Gemara that even in exile Hashem does not reject the Jews, and speaks of the poor whose eyes look to the reading of the Megillah and of raising one's hands to Ribono shel Olam.
Singing.

title.en: Haman's tree and krias shema of the morning

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Amalek brings doubt into emunah. He brings the Pirkei d'Rabbi Eliezer that Haman took his tree from the Kodesh Hakodashim, the place of the point of emunah, and the Yalkut Shimoni that Haman wanted Mordechai hanged in the morning, in order to stop his krias shema of shacharis.

He explains that Haman's descendants in Bnei Brak could keep every mitzvah but could not complete krias shema of the morning, because the klipah of Amalek was not fully destroyed. The Tannaim came, sat all night and repaired them, until it was time for krias shema of shacharis; Bnei Brak, he notes, has the letters of 'boker'.

After singing, the Mashgiach turns to 'parshas hakesef' in the Megillah and to Tosafos, who says Haman's ten thousand kikar of silver were countered by the Jews' half-shekel. He asks about the hundred kikar given in the midbar, and the recording ends.

oneLiner.en: At the Purim seudah the Mashgiach teaches that Purim, a day of the Kodesh HaKodashim beyond all measure, brings a tikkun to everything named in the Megillah, draws all the miracles of its feasts into today's seudah, and belongs above all to the weakest Jews.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Gemara that the place of the Aron took up no space, and says Purim too is beyond measure: a Shabbos in the middle of the week and a day of the Kodesh HaKodashim, whose key is the Megillah, as a story of a soul waiting for Purim shows. From the Gemara's opening verse he explains how Haman gathered the money that went to Mordechai, and that the Megillah repeats in every generation. He explains why Haman and Achashverosh may be named: what is written in Torah returns to its root and is nullified. Through the judgment of Vashti and her later gilgul as a cow that kept Shabbos he shows that Purim brings a tikkun even to her. He then goes through the feasts of the Megillah, the merit of the lechem hapanim and parnasah, and calls Purim the Yom Tov of the nechshalim. On the second side he speaks of rejoicing over Yerushalayim and of holding on to emunah before Moshiach.

en: Like the place of the Aron, which took up no space, Purim is beyond measure: it is a day of the Kodesh HaKodashim, and the Megillah is the key that opens it.

Whatever is written in the Torah, and even more so in the Megillah, is returned to its root and nullified when it is mentioned; therefore saying 'arur Haman' and naming Achashverosh is itself the erasing of Amalek's klipah.
The power of Purim is that it takes what is impure and purifies it: even Vashti, Memuchan and Achashverosh, everyone named in the Megillah, receive their tikkun.
All the miracles of Purim happened at feasts, and all the feasts of the Megillah with their salvations flow into the Purim seudah of every year.

The angel of the lechem hapanim won the Jews' defense because they keep a mitzvah whose reason no one knows, and the lechem hapanim draws down parnasah, so the decree, which threatened life, had to be annulled.
Purim was made for the nechshalim, the weak and fallen; the lower a person is, the closer he is to Purim, and so a generation of many low souls has the greatest Purim.
The Purim seudah repairs the feast of Achashverosh, which celebrated the ruin of Yerushalayim: its main joy is that Yerushalayim will be rebuilt.

candidateTopics: mentioning the name of a rasha

title.en: Purim beyond measure, three days of Shabbos

summary.en: The Mashgiach links the Gemara that the place of the Aron took up no space to the openings of the Megillah that follow it: Purim too is beyond measure. He calls Shabbos, Purim and Shushan Purim three days of Shabbos, since Shabbos, like Hashem, is at war with Amalek.

title.en: The key to the Kodesh HaKodashim

summary.en: Purim is a day of the Kodesh HaKodashim, and one needs a key to enter. The Mashgiach tells of a young man who read the Megillah on the second night of Pesach, and of a soul that had missed the great eis ratzon of Purim. The key, he concludes, is the opening of the Megillah.

title.en: The Gemara's opening, and the Megillah in every generation

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the opening verse from Koheles: the good man is Mordechai, the sinner who gathers is Haman, and it is given to Mordechai and Esther. From the end of the Megillah he shows that it repeats in every generation, with a new Achashverosh, Mordechai and Haman, though not every generation merits a Mordechai like the first.

The Mashgiach asks how 'accepted by most of his brothers', which the Gemara reads as some of the Sanhedrin parting from him, can describe Mordechai, and brings the Chasam Sofer. He explains that the verse speaks of a later Mordechai: the first Mordechai had to build the Beis HaMikdash, so Heaven had Haman collect the money and then gave Haman's house to Mordechai.

title.en: Three world kings, and saying 'arur Haman'

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the Gemara tells that Achav, Achashverosh and Nevuchadnetzar ruled the whole world. He explains that all year one fears to curse a rasha, but Purim is above all accusers, so one may say 'arur Haman'; then he raises a new problem: how may one say a rasha's name at all?

title.en: A name written in the Torah is nullified

summary.en: From the Gemara in Sanhedrin the Mashgiach explains that a name written in the Torah may be said, because the Torah is the root of all holiness and mentioning it returns it to its root and nullifies it. So 'arur Haman' is the erasing of Amalek, and Achashverosh's name is repeated in the Megillah because, as a king over the whole world, his klipah filled the world and is nullified with it.

title.en: Why Vashti was sent to Amon and Moav

summary.en: The Sanhedrin did not want to judge Vashti. The Mashgiach explains that a Jewish court judges for the good, even when it finds a person liable, while others judge as a court of guilt; because Vashti made Jewish girls desecrate Shabbos, the Sanhedrin did not want her judged by Jewish law and sent her to Amon and Moav.

title.en: The Maharal's question, and the cow that kept Shabbos

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Maharal's Ohr Chadash: the salvation came through Vashti's judgment because the Sanhedrin sent it, so the ruling counts as theirs. Then Vashti was judged by a Jewish court after all, and he asks how she merited it. He answers with the Gilgulei Neshamos: Vashti returned as the cow that would not work on Shabbos, whose owner became R' Yochanan ben Torsa.

title.en: Vashti's spark of holiness and the power of Purim

summary.en: Vashti had a spark of holiness, and the Sanhedrin saw it. The Mashgiach brings hints: 'sheshes yamim taavod' spells Vashti, 'ro'ei pnei hamelech' spells parah, and the angel gave her a tail. Memuchan too, whose descendants learned Torah in Bnei Brak, had a spark of holiness. This is the power of Purim, he concludes: it purifies even Vashti and Achashverosh, and all the more those who read the Megillah.
Singing.

title.en: At the tzaddik's table, and the feasts of the Megillah

summary.en: On Purim even a small soul can rise to the chamber of a great tzaddik, so the Mashgiach asks each one to choose a tzaddik and sit at his table. He then explains that all the miracles of Purim happened at feasts, and all those feasts flow into today's seudah; he begins with the first feast, which removed Vashti for 'one better than she'.

The Mashgiach explains the second feast, 'the feast of Esther', as a rest that comes to the world and the raising of the Jews. Then he turns to the feast Esther asked for: whoever merits to sit at the seudah now sits at Esther's feast with Achashverosh and Haman, where Haman can be hanged and Charvonah remembered for good.

title.en: The merit of the lechem hapanim

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara that the angels argued for the Jews with the korbanos, and asks why it was the lechem hapanim, through Memuchan, that decided. Even the Arizal did not know its reason, and the Chinuch brings the Ramban that none is known; the angel argued that the Jews keep a mitzvah without a reason, 'they prepared a table before You'.

The shulchan and the lechem hapanim draw down parnasah, and so does Purim. From the Gemara in Taanis, where praying for parnasah ended a plague because parnasah is given to the living, the Mashgiach explains how the merit of the table annulled the decree of destruction. He ends asking that every Jew be granted abundant parnasah.
Singing.

title.en: The Yom Tov of the nechshalim

summary.en: The Mashgiach contrasts the two verses on the days of Purim, one with Yom Tov and one with gifts to the poor, and says Purim is a special Yom Tov for the nechshalim, the weak whom Amalek attacked. The weaker one is, the closer to Purim; Adar is the month of the small, and the first salvation came through Memuchan, the smallest. He calls to rejoice in the Yom Tov of the nechshalim.
A few words on the joy of the day, followed by a long interlude.

title.en: Achashverosh's feast and the joy of Yerushalayim

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the students of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai: the Jews were condemned for enjoying Achashverosh's feast, which he made because he thought Yerushalayim would never be rebuilt. With the Chasam Sofer he explains that the Purim seudah repairs this: its main joy is Yerushalayim, and one should bind oneself to it and hope for the salvation.

title.en: Holding on to emunah before Moshiach

summary.en: After singing, the Mashgiach brings the sefarim that in the last generation before Moshiach the main ones are those who hold on to emunah and hope for Hashem's salvation; in the time of hester they stay firm. Adar is a month of laughter: they laugh at the nations and their threats, and remain Jews even if they are the last.
An interlude.

title.en: Closing: the longing of the waters

summary.en: The Mashgiach speaks of the lower waters that wanted to be close to the King and were given the water libation and the salt of the korbanos; now that the Beis HaMikdash is destroyed they weep again, and the Jewish heart weeps with them. He closes with the coming of the redemption, as the going out of Egypt.
An interlude until the end of the recording.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains why Avraham Avinu took gifts from Pharaoh but refused the king of Sodom, showing that his descent to Mitzrayim was both wrong and right, and that Pharaoh's gifts were a sign for his children's leaving Mitzrayim with great wealth.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with a contradiction: Avraham Avinu refused any gift from the king of Sodom, yet he told Sarah to say she was his sister so that Pharaoh would give him gifts. He brings the Ramban, who faults Avraham for leaving Eretz Yisrael in the famine and endangering Sarah, and says this caused the exile in Mitzrayim, and he contrasts it with the Zohar, where an angel assured Avraham. He finds the same clash between the Midrash and the Zohar on Yaakov bowing to Esav. To resolve it he explains the four levels of Torah, pshat, remez, drush and sod, which do not always fit together, and shows from halachic examples, fasting for a dream on Shabbos and the nazir's korban, that one act can be both wrong and right. Avraham's descent caused the galus but the galus purified his children. Following the Ramban's rule that the deeds of the fathers are a sign for the children, Pharaoh's gifts sealed that Klal Yisrael would leave Mitzrayim with wealth, while a rasha's money carries his tumah.

en: Avraham refused the king of Sodom's gifts but sought Pharaoh's gifts, an apparent contradiction the Mashgiach sets out to resolve.
The Ramban faults Avraham for going down to Mitzrayim without permission and endangering Sarah, and says this brought the galus of Mitzrayim, while the Zohar says an angel assured him.
The four levels of Torah, pshat, remez, drush and sod, usually fit into one another but sometimes contradict, and both sides can be true.
One act can be both a mitzvah and an aveirah, as with fasting for a dream on Shabbos and the nazir who must bring a korban; the question is which outweighs the other.
Avraham's descent to Mitzrayim was wrong, since it brought the galus, and right, since the galus purified his children.
By the Ramban's principle that the deeds of the fathers are a sign for the children, every stage of Avraham's stay in Mitzrayim foreshadows the exile and redemption of his descendants.
Avraham took Pharaoh's gifts only for his children, to seal that they would leave with wealth, while he refused Sodom's money because a rasha's money carries his tumah.

title.en: Gifts from Pharaoh, none from Sodom

summary.en: The Mashgiach recounts how Avraham rescued Lot and the captives from the four kings and refused anything from the king of Sodom. He contrasts this with Mitzrayim, where Avraham told Sarah to say she was his sister so that he would benefit, and took Pharaoh's gifts.

title.en: The Ramban and the Zohar on going to Mitzrayim

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Ramban, who criticizes Avraham for leaving Eretz Yisrael in the famine and endangering Sarah, and says this caused the galus of Mitzrayim. He notes that the Ramban drew on the Zohar, yet the Zohar says an angel assured Avraham, while elsewhere it says he went without permission, leaving many contradictions.

title.en: Yaakov bowing to Esav; the four levels of Torah

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows the same clash between the Midrash, which faults Yaakov for humbling himself before Esav, and the Zohar, which calls it wise because it made Esav grow haughty to his downfall. He then explains pshat, remez, drush and sod, which usually fit into one another but sometimes contradict.

The Mashgiach brings examples where pshat and sod point different ways and both are right, depending on a person's madreigah. He shows from fasting for a bad dream on Shabbos, and from the nazir who must bring a korban for depriving himself of wine, that one act can be both right and wrong, and concludes that Yaakov knew both views and chose to bow because the benefit outweighed the harm.

The Mashgiach applies this to Avraham: going down to Mitzrayim was wrong, since it brought the galus, yet right, since the servitude of Mitzrayim purified his children and raised them in kedushah. So the Ramban, who says he was wrong and punished, and the Zohar, which says he was right, are both true.

title.en: The deeds of the fathers: a sign for the children

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Ramban's rule that what happened to the Avos is a sign of what will happen to their descendants, and traces the parallels: the famine, Sarah taken by Pharaoh, the plagues that freed her, and Pharaoh's gifts, foreshadowing Klal Yisrael's going down, enslavement, plagues and exodus with wealth. Avraham knew this, so he took the gifts only for his children.

title.en: Sealing the prophecy; the money of a rasha

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the Bris bein haBesarim came before the trip to Mitzrayim, and that a prophecy can change but a symbolic act of the Avos cannot, so Avraham took Pharaoh's money to secure the redemption with wealth. He refused Sodom's money because a rasha's money carries his tumah, and answers why the Yidden could take Mitzrayim's wealth: Hashem purified it, as the passuk in Tehillim indicates.

oneLiner.en: At the Purim seudah the Mashgiach explains how Purim draws the holiness of Shabbos, Yom Kippur and yom tov into the weekday and into galus, and how every enemy of the Jews ends up singing his own song through his downfall.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Megillah as the book that teaches hashgachah pratis, Hashem's hand hidden inside natural events. He then speaks of Shabbos clothes: chassidim in Lublin learned that wearing them clothes a person in the surrounding lights of Shabbos, and Vashti, who wanted Jewish girls to work on Shabbos, first had them remove those clothes. Purim returns these lights even on a weekday. He speaks of the heavenly chamber opened only through song, of wine and its holiness, of the first drizzle of teshuvah before the geulah, and of Purim as a Ne'ilah greater than Yom Kippur. In the second part he explains that the plans of the wicked fall on their own heads, that Mordechai wanted Purim to be a full yom tov while the other sages kept it a weekday yom tov for galus, and that the ten sons of Haman are written as a shirah, because the downfall of a rasha is his song.

en: The Megillah teaches a Jew to see Hashem's guidance hidden inside events that look natural.
Shabbos clothes clothe a Jew in the makifim, the surrounding lights, of Shabbos, and Purim brings these lights back even on a weekday.
Purim is like Yom Kippur and even greater, and its last hours are a Ne'ilah that must be used.
The plans the wicked make against the Jews turn against them, as Haman's own advice brought about his downfall.
Mordechai wanted Purim to be a full yom tov with a ban on work, but the Jews accepted it as a weekday yom tov that brings holiness into galus.
Every creature's existence is a shirah to Hashem, and a rasha sings his shirah through his downfall, which is why the ten sons of Haman are written as a song.
