summary.en: The opening of the seudah.

The Mashgiach brings the Anshei Knesses HaGedolah on Hashem's awesome deeds and explains that the Megillah teaches a Jew to see Hashem's guidance hidden in every event. He brings the Ba'al Shem Tov that Hashem is hidden within what happens, and that the Jewish people are not left to chance.
An interlude.

title.en: Shabbos clothes and the lights of Shabbos

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of chassidim in Lublin who wondered where their Shabbos feeling came from, and of their Rebbe's explanation that Shabbos clothes clothe a person in the makifim of Shabbos. He brings Chazal on Ruth that her garments were Shabbos clothes, and explains that Vashti, wanting Jewish girls to work on Shabbos, first made them take off their Shabbos clothes.

title.en: Vashti's punishment and Purim's Shabbos lights

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Vashti was punished measure for measure, losing her own garments, and that through Purim the Jews merited to receive the makifim of Shabbos again, even on a weekday.

The Mashgiach speaks of a high chamber in heaven that can be opened only through song, standing next to the chamber of teshuvah, so that one can rise through song as through teshuvah. Shabbos is the chamber of song, and he brings a Midrash about the power of Jews singing together on Shabbos.
An interlude.

title.en: Wine and the Name of Hashem

summary.en: The Mashgiach speaks about wine: he connects it by gematria to the Name of Hashem and to the brachah that comes with kiddush on Shabbos, and explains that the Sages commanded drinking on Purim so that it should be for a brachah.
An interlude.

title.en: The drizzle of teshuvah before the geulah

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara that a heavy rain is preceded by a light drizzle, and says that the teshuvah of his time is that drizzle before the geulah and the building of the Beis HaMikdash. He tells what Rav Yosef Chaim Sonnenfeld answered about building a mikveh, and connects Mordechai to the coming Beis HaMikdash.
An interlude.

title.en: The seudah, wine in the bones, and Purim's Ne'ilah

summary.en: The Mashgiach contrasts the wine of the seudah hamafsekes before Tisha b'Av, of which it says that their sins are upon their bones, with the wine of Purim, which is absorbed into the bones for good and becomes a foundation of joy for the whole year. He explains that Purim is like Yom Kippur and greater, and that its last hours are a Ne'ilah.
Singing.

title.en: The plans of the wicked fall on themselves

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains how Haman's own counsel brought about his downfall: the gallows he prepared became his own. He says that the wicked of every time, naming the leaders of his day, sit and plan against the Jews, but their plans come from foolish heads and lead to the geulah.

The Mashgiach brings the Gemara that Haman, who had been a barber for twenty-two years, himself cut Mordechai's hair, since Esther had sent the barbers away. He asks how Mordechai could let a gentile cut his hair, and speaks of the Arizal on the tzelem Elokim in every person.

The Mashgiach brings the Gemara that Mordechai made the first day of Pesach a fast, and explains that Mordechai, knowing of the miracle of Purim, moved the yom tov of Pesach into Purim, with Shabbos clothes, eating and drinking. He then brings the passuk of the days of feasting and joy and the Gemara that the Jews did not accept the day as a yom tov.

title.en: Mordechai's yom tov and the weekday yom tov of galus

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Mordechai wanted Purim to be a yom tov with a ban on work, greater than Yom Kippur, because as a spark of Moshe Rabbeinu he stood above galus. The other sages, who were in galus, wanted a weekday yom tov to bring holiness into the weekday and into galus, and so its joy is in gifts to the poor; in the future Purim will be a full yom tov.
The opening of the second part of the seudah.
A song.
An interlude.

title.en: The shirah of the ten sons of Haman

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the ten sons of Haman are written in the form of a shirah. He explains that every creature sings shirah by doing what Hashem created it for, and that a rasha's shirah is his downfall. This, he says, is the meaning of saying 'blessed is Haman': a blessing that the enemies of the Jews sing their song.
An interlude.

The Mashgiach asks why Belshazzar was killed the night he used the vessels of the Beis HaMikdash, while Achashverosh, who did the same, was not. He answers that Achashverosh, a hater of the Jews, received a worse punishment: he was forced from heaven to do good for the Jews and to honor Mordechai. So too all who want to harm the Jews will be forced to do them good.
An interlude.

title.en: L'chaim and wishes for the yeshuah

summary.en: The Mashgiach says that since it is still Purim one should drink l'chaim and wish that the Jews have a yeshuah. He connects the gathering with the tzaddikim in Yerushalayim, where the Megillah is now being read, and wishes for the great yeshuah.

oneLiner.en: At the Purim seudah the Mashgiach teaches that even in the deepest hester panim, in a palace of klipah, Hashem loves and remembers every Jew, and that Purim reaches the place where everything can be turned to good.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by saying that Purim is above time, as shown by Jerusalem's Purim on a later day. Achashverosh's feast was an imitation of the Beis HaMikdash, a palace of klipah; Esther guarded Shabbos there, and her greenish look with a thread of grace shows Klal Yisrael in hester panim, still loved by Hashem, who goes down to His bride even in a house of idols. The extra Jews left out of Haman's silver and forgotten by Moshe are the forgotten ones before Moshiach, yet Hashem remembers them, as the thirteenth month of a leap year shows. Because David accepted Shimi's curse as from Hashem, Mordechai came from Shimi and defeated Amalek's belief in chance. Purim reaches the place where din turns to rachamim, and every year one must go in before the King and cry out to Him.

en: Purim is above time, and Jerusalem, which reads the Megillah on a day that is not the day of the miracle, holds its highest level.
Achashverosh's palace was a Beis HaMikdash of klipah, and Esther had to guard the memory of Shabbos there at every moment.
Even when Klal Yisrael is in a house of idols, Hashem goes down to His bride out of great love and sees a hidden beauty in every Jew.
The Jews outside the camp, whom even Moshe forgot, are the Jews before Moshiach, and Hashem remembers them in their lowliness.
Nothing in the world is chance; Amalek's aim is to make Jews forget hashgacha pratis, and Purim teaches the opposite.
Purim's light comes from a place where everything can still be turned around, where din becomes rachamim and mourning becomes joy.
The Megillah is not past history: every year Hashem gives permission anew to come before Him, and one must go in and cry out.

candidateTopics: Achashverosh's feast and the Beis HaMikdash
Hashem's love for Klal Yisrael in exile

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens with the hidden depth of Purim and the verse about a person in honor who does not understand: one can be given so precious a time and not grasp it. He blesses that Mordechai and Esther be advocates for all Jews, and turns to the Mishnah's list of days on which the Megillah is read.

He finds a hint in the first sage named in the tractate to the sun, from which all times come. Jerusalem reads the Megillah on a day that was not the day of the miracle, which shows that its Purim is above time and is the highest level of Purim.

title.en: Achashverosh's imitation of the Beis HaMikdash

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Achashverosh's feast was meant to imitate the Beis HaMikdash: to show the Jews that they have no Mikdash and no king, while he has its vessels and the priestly garments. It was a Beis HaMikdash of klipah. He adds that the miracle of the Megillah came against Haman's design.

title.en: Esther guards Shabbos in the palace

summary.en: He brings the Gemara that Esther counted the days by her seven maidens so as to know when Shabbos is. Vashti was the klipah against Shabbos, so Esther named the maidens in order not to forget Shabbos for a moment. That time was just before the redemption, like today, and he says such a guard is needed now too.

title.en: Greenish, with a thread of grace

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara that Esther was greenish with a thread of grace drawn over her, and explains that she was the symbol of Klal Yisrael in that time of hester panim, when Jews had enjoyed the king's feast. Even in that state Hashem sees a hidden beauty in every Jew, and this is also the meaning of her name Hadassah.

title.en: The King goes down to His bride

summary.en: When Esther entered the house of idols the Shechinah left her and she cried out to Hashem. The Mashgiach brings the Zera Kodesh's parable of a king who leaves his throne to go to his bride in a foul place, to show his great love, and applies it to Hashem's love for Klal Yisrael in exile.

title.en: Mizmor l'Dovid in the house of idols

summary.en: He reads Mizmor l'Dovid, 'Hashem is my shepherd', 'in green pastures', and 'though I walk in the valley of the shadow of death' as the house of idols, where Hashem is with a Jew. Today too Jews stand in a house of idols just before Moshiach; he speaks of how precious a Jew is there and of emunah in the coming of Moshiach.
An interlude.

title.en: Haman's silver and the forgotten Jews

summary.en: He brings Tosafos' question on Haman's ten thousand kikar of silver against the shekalim. The Mashgiach explains that the extra Jews, whose shekalim did not go into the sockets of the Mishkan, were those outside the camp from shevet Dan, whom Moshe forgot, until, as the Megaleh Amukos says, the soul of Rabbi Akiva reminded him.

The Mashgiach explains that even one poor in mitzvos is answered, and that before Moshiach the Jews are the forgotten ones outside the camp, yet Hashem remembers them. He ties this to Adar, the lowest month, to this year's Purim in a leap year, and to the added 'atonement of sin' in the thirteenth month.
An interlude.

He asks why Mordechai did not enter the palace himself after Hasach was killed, and explains that he could not go into a place of klipah and stood by the water. He tells of a Lechovitcher chassid who immersed in the river in Petersburg, and concludes that Hashem's kingship reaches even the lowest places.
An interlude.

title.en: Shimi ben Gera and the end of chance

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that David accepted Shimi ben Gera's curse as coming from Hashem, since nothing in the world is chance. Amalek wants Jews to believe in chance; because David let Shimi live, Mordechai descended from him and brought the miracle of Purim. Through this David became the fourth leg of the Merkavah and his name gained a yud.
An interlude.

title.en: Loving Hashem and a Jew; din turned to mercy

summary.en: He says one knows how much one loves Hashem by how much one loves a Jew, which is the meaning of mishloach manos. He brings the Gemara on 'to know what this is' and the luchos written on both sides, and shows that Haman's words hold Hashem's Name reversed while Esther's words hold it in order, turning din into rachamim.

title.en: Purim reaches the place of turning

summary.en: He explains the Mishnah's reversed order of days as the secret of Purim, turning din into rachamim. He brings the Ohev Yisrael that Purim's light comes from the 'world of the unformed', where everything can still be reshaped, like dough before it is baked. Mordechai and Esther reached there, the level of the Kodesh HaKodashim, where mourning turns to joy.

title.en: A King who brings the distant near

summary.en: The Mashgiach speaks of a king who brings near the distant ones first, and says that Jews have such a King. He pleads that Hashem bring near first those who are far.

title.en: Going in before the King today

summary.en: He says Purim must also have a serious moment. He brings the Midrash that Esther passed seven guarded chambers to reach the king, who in the inner sense is Hashem. The sefarim teach that one who reads the Megillah as past history has not fulfilled it; every year Hashem gives permission anew, and one must go in and cry out to Him.

After a story about a large appeal where money poured like water, the Mashgiach contrasts a Megillah sold all year as a cheap Purim story-book with a Megillah written as holy writing. He closes with Adar as the last and lowest month.
Singing.

oneLiner.en: At the Purim seudah the Mashgiach explains that the turnabout of Purim comes from Hashem's love and from a place above time, and that Purim was made above all for the Jews who are pushed away and stand outside, longing to come in.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach begins with Achashverosh, who spoke to Esther only through an interpreter until she revealed her descent from Shaul; once he spoke to her directly he turned around completely. The kelipah of Achashverosh, he explains, is the lack of connection, and Jews coming together breaks it. The Megillah speaks to us face to face, like Matan Torah. The turnabout of Purim comes from Hashem's love, as Bilam's curse was turned into a blessing. He speaks of Vashti and the crown of royalty, then explains that Purim was made for the far-off ones and comes from Olam Haba, which is not bound to time; hence the Megillah's many dates and the old wine at Achashverosh's feast. The villagers' early reading becomes a lesson about the descendants of Dan, who always have a din Torah. He closes with Charvona's turnabout and with the walled city whose laws reach the places near it.

en: The kelipah of Achashverosh is the lack of a direct connection, and when Jews come together in a bond with one another it is broken.
The whole turnabout of Purim stems from Hashem's love for the Jews, as with Bilam's curse that Hashem turned into a blessing.
Purim was made for the far-off and pushed-away Jews, and it is the last chance for those who did not get there earlier in the year.
Following the Maharal, Purim comes from Olam Haba, which is not limited by time; this is why the Megillah has so many dates of reading.
We are all like the people of Shevet Dan, cast out of the camp and far into galus, and we have a din Torah with Hashem, Who listens when one comes to Him with one.
The power of Purim can turn around even a Jew who is completely dried out from Yiddishkeit, as Charvona turned around.

title.en: Achashverosh speaks to Esther face to face

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Achashverosh spoke to Esther through an interpreter until she told him she descended from Shaul, and then he turned around completely. The kelipah of Achashverosh is the lack of connection, and Jews coming together break it.

title.en: The Megillah speaks face to face

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the Megillah, written by Esther and Mordechai, speaks to us face to face like Matan Torah, a fiery Purim. He discusses Esther's request to delay until the next day and says the whole wonder of Purim comes from a very high place, as the holy Maggid says.

title.en: The turnabout comes from Hashem's love

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the main thing a Jew must know is that Hashem loves the Jews. He traces the turnabout of Purim back to Bilam and Balak, when Hashem turned the curse into a blessing because He loves His people.
An interlude.

title.en: Gathering to recognize the Jewish soul

summary.en: The Mashgiach speaks of how dear a Jew is to Hashem and reads the words of the Megillah about gathering and standing for their lives as gathering together to recognize what a Jewish soul is.

title.en: Vashti and the crown of royalty

summary.en: The Mashgiach speaks of the command to bring Vashti with the crown of royalty, recalls how Belshazzar was killed the night of his feast, and brings the Gemara on what happened to Vashti before she was to come. He explains that the Jews' crown of royalty is Shabbos, which Vashti wanted to take from them by forcing Jewish girls to work on Shabbos.
An interlude.

title.en: Purim for the far-off, from Olam Haba

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the many dates of Purim were made for the far-off ones, for whom Purim is the last chance. Bringing the Maharal, he says Purim comes from Olam Haba, which is not bound to time, and this is why the first halachah of the Megillah lists so many days of reading.

The Mashgiach asks why the Megillah tells that at Achashverosh's feast each guest drank wine older than himself, and explains that old wine is a hint to Olam Haba, which comes from before the world, the days of old.

The Mashgiach asks why the villagers were allowed to read early on the day they come to town for the beis din, when few people go to a din Torah. He answers that Purim was made for the far-off ones, the people of Dan, who always have a din Torah, as the Gemara in Pesachim and the din Torah of the son of the Danite woman show.

The Mashgiach says that we, far off in galus, are all like the people of Dan and must cry out to Hashem that we have a din Torah with Him and ask when the day of ingathering will come. The name Dan comes from the words 'Hashem has judged me and also heard my voice', and he adds that our generation serves Hashem from the lowest levels.
An interlude.

title.en: Charvona and the power of Purim

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Charvona was with Haman, yet when he saw the turn he turned around, and his name changed from an alef to a heh. The power of Purim can transform even a Jew who is completely dried out, since every Jew is a child of Avraham Avinu, whose name was changed.

title.en: Near and visible to the walled city

summary.en: The Mashgiach points out that only by Purim does a place near and visible to a walled city share its laws. He explains that Purim is for those who stood outside the camp, near it and longing to come in; Hashem gathered their longing, and so a place near and visible receives the laws of the city.
The seudah continues.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that on Rosh Hashanah, through the shofar and the pesukim of Malchiyos, Zichronos and Shofros, Klal Yisrael draws down the Thirteen Attributes of Mercy and creates a new world, as Hashem saved Noach out of love, and that the day is to be met with simcha and with tefillos for Klal Yisrael and the whole world.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the introduction to Zichronos, which says Hashem remembered Noach with love, and asks what love there was if the flood and Noach's survival were planned from the start. He traces the world from Adam in Gan Eden through the sin and the ten corrupt generations, and explains that Hashem planned a new world of tzaddikim to emerge from the teiva, but Cham, the dog and the raven sinned there and ruined the plan. Hashem kept Noach alive out of love, foreseeing Avraham and Klal Yisrael. That love flows from the Thirteen Attributes, which Klal Yisrael draws down with the shofar and the thirty pesukim, creating a new world as with the ten utterances. He then stresses the regular davening as the essence, tells of the Klausenberger Rebbe choosing Kriyas HaTorah over shofar, explains the Akeidah as Yitzchak's victory over Yishmael, brings the Chasam Sofer's parable on simcha in judgment, and closes with Malchus and tefillah for the world in a dangerous time.

en: Hashem kept Noach and the creatures in the teiva alive out of love even after the plan of a new world of tzaddikim was ruined, because He foresaw Avraham and Klal Yisrael.

On Rosh Hashanah Klal Yisrael creates a new world through the ten pesukim each of Malchiyos, Zichronos and Shofros, corresponding to the ten utterances of creation, and through the shofar, which draws down the Thirteen Attributes of Mercy.
The sound of the shofar has no words; it is above speech like the utterance of Bereishis, and like the breath Hashem blew into Adam.
The regular davening is the essence of the Rosh Hashanah tefillah, and the piyutim are an addition that cannot stand without it.
The Akeidah, read on the second day, was Yitzchak's victory over Yishmael, who is called an enemy, worse than Eisav.
On Rosh Hashanah Hashem judges Jews by what they truly are in their neshamah, so the day is to be approached with simcha and confidence.
In a year of dangers for Klal Yisrael and all mankind, the Mashgiach says the tefillos of Rosh Hashanah must be for Klal Yisrael and for the entire world.

candidateTopics: simcha on the day of judgment

title.en: Why Noach was remembered with love

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the Zichronos introduction praises Hashem for remembering Noach with love when the flood was planned from the start. He traces the world from Gan Eden through the sin and ten corrupt generations to the flood, and explains that a new world of tzaddikim was meant to emerge from the teiva, but Cham, the dog and the raven sinned there; Hashem saved them anyway out of love, foreseeing Avraham and Klal Yisrael.

title.en: The shofar creates a new world

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Noach went out into a world that was not yet perfect, and that his survival flowed from the Thirteen Attributes of Mercy, which Klal Yisrael arouses on Rosh Hashanah. With the ten pesukim of each blessing, corresponding to the ten utterances, and with the shofar, a wordless sound above speech like the utterance of Bereishis and like the breath blown into Adam, a new world is created.

title.en: The regular davening and the Klausenberger's choice

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the regular davening, from Pesukei D'Zimra through the blessings of Krias Shema, is the essence of Rosh Hashanah and the piyutim are only an addition. He then tells how the Klausenberger Rebbe, old and weak, chose to lein the Torah rather than blow shofar, so as to arouse in Heaven Sarah's words that Yishmael must be driven out and have no share in Eretz Yisrael with Yitzchak.

title.en: The Akeidah as Yitzchak's victory over Yishmael

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the Akeidah, read on the second day, came about through Yishmael's boast to Yitzchak about his milah at thirteen, and Yitzchak's answer that he was ready to give his whole being; the Akeidah showed a mesiras nefesh Yishmael cannot match. He adds that Yishmael is called an enemy, worse than Eisav, who is only called a hater.

title.en: Simcha on the day of judgment

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that on Rosh Hashanah Hashem judges Jews by what they are in their neshamah, so the day is met with simcha and confidence. He brings the Chasam Sofer's parable of an imprisoned minister who rejoiced on the king's coronation day, his own day of judgment, and was pardoned and promoted, and says this joy in the King is a Jew's strength in judgment.

title.en: Accepting Malchus in a year of dangers

summary.en: The Mashgiach says that in proclaiming Hashem's Malchus over the world one must include oneself and accept it. He describes the coming year as one of dangers for Klal Yisrael and the world, brings the passuk in Yeshayahu about Egyptian fighting Egyptian, city against city, which he connects to what is seen now, probably in Syria, and concludes that the tefillos must be for Jews and for the whole world.

The Mashgiach brings the Chiddushei HaRim that Rosh Hashanah is for the entire world while Yom Kippur is between Hashem and Klal Yisrael, and warns of madmen who could destroy the world. He relates a tradition from tzaddikim that before Moshiach the nations will be dragged into war against their will, and closes with a call to daven for Klal Yisrael, the world and one's family, and with the tefillah for the honor of Klal Yisrael.

oneLiner.en: At the Purim seudah the Mashgiach teaches that the beauty of Klal Yisroel lies in the faith of its lowest, last generations, and that a Jew who learns to read the Megillah sees Hashem's hand in every event, including the wonders of his own day.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by asking everyone to bind themselves with all Jews. He explains that Haman, casting his lot, touched a holy goral that brought Purim into the world, and that Mordechai, who stepped on Haman, carries in his name the 'midrach' of 've-atah al bamoseimo tidroch', the last words of Moshe Rabbeinu's blessing. A Jew learns to read the Megillah, and history, as a doctor reads an x-ray, seeing Hashem in every event; he points to the wonders of the current war around Iraq. From Shir HaShirim he shows that the kallah's beauty is counted from the feet: the emunah of the lowest generation is Hashem's greatest delight. In the second part he speaks of the mistaken calculations of the end, Esther drawing the level of yechidah into Purim, the holy spark hidden even in Haman and Amalek, and the Purim seudah as a seudah of Olam Haba.

en: Haman's lot was a holy goral that fixed the days of Purim, which will never be nullified, and touching it is a great joy.
One who learns to read the Megillah sees Ribono shel Olam in every word of it and in every event of history, the way a doctor reads an x-ray.
The kallah, Klal Yisroel, is praised from the feet upward, because her main beauty is the emunah of the lowest, last generations.
Esther drew the level of yechidah, which every Jew touches for a moment on Yom Kippur, into Purim, so that even the lowest Jew can reach it.
Even Haman and Amalek hold a holy spark, a spark of desire for closeness to kedushah, from which converts and Torah scholars later came.
A Jew who sees Hashem in every detail and thanks Him for it is truly living.

candidateTopics: the Gulf War as a miracle

title.en: Bound with all Jews at the seudah

summary.en: The Mashgiach says that when all Jews do something together, one helps the other and it grows stronger, and asks everyone to bind themselves now with the Jews in Yerushalayim, where the main simchah is, the simchah Esther drew down. Purim's purpose, he adds, is to bring in even the lowest levels.

title.en: Haman's joy and the holy goral

summary.en: He brings the Gemara that Haman rejoiced greatly when his lot fell in the month of Moshe Rabbeinu's passing, and explains that Haman had touched something holy: a goral, like the lots of Yom Kippur, that fixed the days of Purim, which will never be nullified. He exclaims what a joy it is to touch that goral today.

The Mashgiach notes that Adar is the month of the tribe of Naftali, whose Nasi was Achira ben Einan. He reads 'Achira' as 'my brother', the theme of mishloach manos between Jews and between Hashem and the Jews, and 'Einan' as the Jews being the apple of Hashem's eye.
An interlude in the seudah.

After words about the yom tov of malchus, the Mashgiach tells how Haman had to help Mordechai onto the horse, and Mordechai stepped on him and kicked him. When Haman protested, Mordechai answered that this applies to Jews, but about you it says 've-atah al bamoseimo tidroch', the last words of Moshe Rabbeinu.

He explains that 'tidroch', the last word of Moshe's blessing, is the final point of the soul of Klal Yisroel. He connects it to the passuk 'ad midrach kaf ragel' and shows that the name Mordechai holds the word 'midrach'. He calls on everyone to accept ol malchus shamayim now, together with all Jews and the tzaddikim of Yerushalayim.
An interlude in the seudah.

title.en: Moshe's words and telling Hashem's wonders

summary.en: The Mashgiach speaks of the first and last words of Moshe Rabbeinu and of Mordechai carrying Moshe Rabbeinu's quality, as the Megaleh Amukos brings from a Midrash. He then speaks of the mitzvah to sing and tell all of Hashem's wonders, and of a man who spent whole nights alone in the beis medrash singing 'shiru lo zamru lo'.

Hashem's name is not written in the Megillah, so a non-Jew reading it would see only a story; a believing Jew sees Ribono shel Olam in every word. The Mashgiach compares this to an x-ray: a simple person sees only lines, while the doctor can read it.

One who learns to read the Megillah sees Hashem in history, in the events of the klal and of every individual, even between the lines of the newspapers. Hidden miracles are greater than open ones, he says; a Jew who thanks Hashem for every detail truly lives, and this is what 'Echad' means.

title.en: Today's wonders: Iraq, Kuwait and America

summary.en: The Mashgiach sees open wonders in current events: the enemy entered Kuwait first rather than Eretz Yisroel, and America, which armed itself for thirty years against Russia, found Russia collapsed and siding with it, so the preparation turned out to protect Eretz Yisroel. The Megillah, he says, is now being written; he brings that Yishmael will be the last exile, and speaks of telling Hashem's wonders and remembering Amalek.
An interlude in the seudah.

Shir HaShirim praises the chassan, Hashem, from the head downward, and the kallah, Klal Yisroel, from the feet upward. Going down the generations from Moshe Rabbeinu to today's dark generation, the Mashgiach explains that the greatest beauty is a Jew today who falls and gets soiled, yet grabs hold of himself, cries out that there is a Creator, and holds on to a bit of Torah, tefillah and good deeds.

title.en: Mah yafu pe'amayich and the last day

summary.en: The kallah's main beauty is the lowest levels. Hashem loved Esther's generation above all generations of tzaddikim, and 'va-tischak le-yom acharon' speaks of a Jew in the last generation. Hashem showed Moshe 'the last day': how, despite apikorsus and pritzus, Jews will remain Jews and hold on to emunah.
A Jew needs two laughs, the Mashgiach says: everyone laughs at him, and he laughs at the world. In the last day, when all laugh at the Jews, they laugh back.

The Mashgiach tells the Midrash of a Jew's cow, sold to a non-Jew, that would not work on Shabbos until its former owner spoke into its ear; the non-Jew converted and became Rabbi Yochanan ben Torsa. He then brings that when Rabbi Akiva thought Ben Koziva was Moshiach, Rabbi Yochanan ben Torsa told him grass would grow on his cheeks and Moshiach would still not have come.

title.en: Calculating the end, the last test, Daniel's longing

summary.en: He explains that Achashverosh made his feast once he calculated that the seventy years were over and the Beis Hamikdash would not be rebuilt, and that the Jews who attended were punished; even Daniel erred in the calculation, and the confusion weakened the Jews' hope for Moshiach. He compares today's last test of Klal Yisroel to the Akeidah, Avraham Avinu's last test, which was to follow Hashem without understanding. Finally he describes Daniel's longing for the geulah, which led him to search the calculation in the sefarim.

title.en: Esther and the level of yechidah

summary.en: Purim, the Mashgiach explains, is for those who have fallen lowest. On Yom Kippur every Jew touches for a moment the level of yechidah; Esther drew this level into Purim so that even the lowest Jew can reach it, and she drew down malchus when she stood in the inner court of the king's house.

title.en: The wine of Purim and Olam Haba

summary.en: He explains the drinking of wine on Purim: a spark of holiness lies within the kelipah and must be raised. The Purim seudah is a seudah of Olam Haba, and its wine is likened to the wine stored away for the World to Come.

title.en: Timna and the holy spark in Haman

summary.en: He brings the Gemara that Menashe mocked the passuk 've-achos Lotan Timna', and the Rambam that this passuk is as holy as any other. Timna, a king's daughter, wanted to join Avraham and was turned away, and Amalek came from her. He reads 'tzorer ha-Yehudim' as binding together: Haman held a holy spark, and from his descendants came converts who learned Torah, among them Rabbi Shmuel bar Shilas.

title.en: Amalek's spark of closeness; the queen trembles

summary.en: Amalek's whole life-force is a spark of kiruv, a desire to come close to holiness, yet he attacks the weak who fell behind the camp. The Mashgiach reads 'va-tischalchal ha-malkah me'od' as Klal Yisroel trembling over the chillul Hashem of the day: the old ruler returns to his throne, so what of Melech HaMashiach? He closes by calling to join all Jews at the Purim seudah, a seudah of Olam Haba, and the Jews of Yerushalayim.
An interlude in the seudah, with a few closing words.

oneLiner.en: At the Purim seudah the Mashgiach teaches that Purim, the day of Mordechai who descended into the depths of exile and never forgot Yerushalayim, already carries the light of Moshiach, and that every Jew who binds himself to it is turned over and reborn.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by calling Purim a serious time to ask for great things. Mordechai, who knew all seventy languages, went down into every klipah of exile; the Gemara identifies him with Malachi, the last prophet, who spoke of the final redemption. Jews are holy to Hashem, and the days of Purim end in the geulah. The seudah expresses the bond with Yerushalayim, and true bitachon brings parnassah, as a story of Rebbe Nachman shows. Mordechai, 'doresh tov l'amo', is a likeness of Moshiach; the Beis Hamikdash, burned with fire, will be rebuilt with fire by the King. Mordechai is 'Ish Yemini' because he remembered Yerushalayim. Adar has already been turned over, and the other months will follow. In the second part he speaks of the gate for all the tribes through which Moshiach will come, of the wine of Purim, and closes that every Jew becomes newborn.

en: Mordechai knew all the languages because he had to go down into every klipah of exile, each language being its own klipah.
Mordechai is Malachi, the last prophet who spoke about the end of days, and he went down into the depths of the generation.
The main seudah is eaten at night, when the Purim of Yerushalayim begins, because the seudah is a joining with Yerushalayim.
Mordechai is called Ish Yemini because he never forgot Yerushalayim.
The Beis Hamikdash, destroyed by fire through a king, will be rebuilt with fire through the King.
Adar has already been turned over from sorrow to joy, and the other months of mourning are still waiting to be turned over.
A Jew who binds himself to Purim becomes like a newborn, fresh and pure.

candidateTopics: rebuilding the Beis Hamikdash with fire
the gate for all the tribes

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens with the words 'kiymu v'kiblu hayehudim', saying that each one should accept upon himself anew before the Ribono shel Olam.

title.en: Mordechai who knew all the languages

summary.en: The Mashgiach says that now is a serious time to ask for great things. He brings the Gemara that Mordechai knew all seventy languages, explains that each language is a klipah, and says Mordechai went down into all of them. He adds that Mordechai is Malachi.

title.en: Malachi, the last prophet, and the descent into exile

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Malachi was the last prophet, who spoke to the Jews of the end of days. Like Yosef, who had to know all the languages, Mordechai went down into the depths of the exile and broke a path through it, and he brought the days of Purim down to the lowest levels.
An interlude.
The Mashgiach says that Jews are holy to Hashem and are no one's ransom, and that whoever says otherwise is a rasha. The days of Purim, he says, end in the geulah.

title.en: Bound to Yerushalayim from outside it

summary.en: The Mashgiach speaks of Amalek, who attacks the Jews when they are bound to Eretz Yisrael and Yerushalayim, and says that even outside Yerushalayim Jews are bound to it. They have gathered today because 'My eyes and My heart shall be there all the days'.
An interlude.

title.en: Bitachon and parnassah: Rebbe Nachman's story

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes a Jew who sits and learns, fixes times for Torah and then goes to work, and says he will lose nothing: what is meant for him will come. He tells a story Rebbe Nachman of Breslov related about a merchant who held on to his bitachon when he lost everything, and was rewarded with a great fortune.
An interlude.

title.en: Mordechai, 'doresh tov l'amo', a likeness of Moshiach

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the Jews saw in Mordechai a likeness of Moshiach, and that Purim is the eighth light, beyond the seven. He explains that 'doresh tov l'amo', the last pasuk of the Megillah, refers to Melech HaMoshiach, and brings a Midrash that Achashverosh alludes to the Ribono shel Olam, Who is the last and the first.

title.en: Rebuilt with fire by the King

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the Beis Hamikdash can only be destroyed and built by a king, bringing the Gemara in Bava Basra. From the Gemara in Bava Kamma he shows that Hashem, Who burned it with fire, will rebuild it with fire, and he ties this to Adar and to 'Adir bamarom Hashem'.
An interlude.

title.en: The night seudah and Mordechai Ish Yemini

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Chasam Sofer that the mitzvah of the seudah corrects the Jews' enjoyment of Achashverosh's feast, and says the main seudah is at night when Yerushalayim's Purim begins. From 'Im eshkachech Yerushalayim' he explains that Mordechai is called Ish Yemini because he remembered Yerushalayim, and closes with 'Yemin Hashem romemah'.
An interlude.

title.en: The month that was turned over

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Adar has already been turned over, while the fasts of Tammuz, Av and Teves still wait to become days of joy. Purim belongs to the days of Moshiach, and the Jews of the last generation will be turned over, the lowest becoming the highest. He calls on everyone to turn himself over today.

title.en: The Purim of Yerushalayim, like the shliach tzibbur

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Arizal that the tefillah of the shliach tzibbur is always accepted, and says the Purim of Yerushalayim is like it, a higher joy. This is why Esther asked for another day, 'la'asos kedas hayom'.
Singing.

title.en: The gate for all the tribes

summary.en: The Mashgiach speaks of the twelve gates of the Beis Hamikdash for the twelve tribes and a thirteenth for one who does not know his tribe, and links it to the nusach of the Ba'al Shem Tov. Adar Sheni, when the Purim miracle happened, is such an all-including gate, where all Jews join as one soul. Moshiach will come through this gate and gather the forgotten ones.
An interlude.

title.en: The King who went down for His bride

summary.en: The Mashgiach says wine is the first and the lowest, reaching down to the lowest place. He brings a mashal of a king who went into a lowly place because his bride was there, the Ribono shel Olam with Knesses Yisrael. He says the wine of Purim brings down the light of Melech HaMoshiach, and that Eliyahu Hanavi comes on Purim.
The Mashgiach says that on Purim one must drink wine, for now there are great lights. He speaks of Adar as a month of increased joy and of the Jewish home as a Beis Hamikdash, and turns to Shabbos.
An interlude.

The Mashgiach closes that the kingdom of Heaven will be revealed over the whole world and the Jews will be born anew, 'l'am nolad'. Every Jew who binds himself to Purim becomes a newborn, fresh and pure.
The end of the seudah.

oneLiner.en: At the Purim seudah the Mashgiach teaches that a Jew in exile rejoices with Jerusalem, that the inner content of what Jews give is fire, and that Mordechai, by standing with his people, turned Knesses Yisrael's complaint into the miracle of Purim.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Purim of Jerusalem: the Jews of the exile rejoice together with Jerusalem, and Purim will remain even in the days of Moshiach. He discusses eruv tavshilin and forgetting, and the altar of earth that must be attached, as Purim was fixed for all generations. Mordechai, the 'ish yemini', declares at Achashverosh's feast that he belongs to Jerusalem. Haman's fall is a biur chametz, and the whole Seder night is matzah. Jews are children of Hashem, so on Purim one gives to all. The inner meaning of kesef is fire: the difference between Yisrael and Amalek is 'aish'. He explains Knesses Yisrael's complaint against Mordechai through Rav's merit and the Yismach Moshe. On the second side he discusses the proofs that the Megillah was said with ruach hakodesh, Amalek's 'chance', the wine of Jerusalem and the song of Shabbos.

en: When Jerusalem celebrates its Purim, the Jews in exile rejoice together with Jerusalem, for every Jew belongs to Jerusalem.
Jews are children of Hashem, and a father wants others to have mercy on his child; therefore on Purim one gives to everyone.
The inner content of the money a Jew gives is the love and fire with which he gives it, 'tocho ratzuf ahavah', and from this the Beis HaMikdash was built.
The difference between Yisrael and Amalek is 'aish', fire, which Haman's money could not extinguish.
Knesses Yisrael's complaint against Mordechai is explained through the merit of a tzaddik who stands within the decree together with the people.
Shmuel's proof that the Megillah was said with ruach hakodesh, 'kiymu v'kiblu', rests on emunah and is better than proofs from reasoning.

candidateTopics: the goral of Purim and Yom Kippur

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Purim of Shushan and of Jerusalem: now that Jerusalem celebrates its Purim, the Jews in exile rejoice together with Jerusalem. He cites the Rambam that Purim will remain in the days of Moshiach, and the passuk that Hashem will be a wall of fire around Jerusalem.
Interlude.

The Mashgiach explains that an eruv tavshilin is made so that the joy of Yom Tov should not make one forget Shabbos, and brings the Imrei Emes's question whether a Purim on Erev Shabbos would need one. He asks where forgetting comes from, noting that there is no forgetting before Hashem's Throne, and says that on Purim one does not forget.

title.en: The altar of earth: attached and fixed

summary.en: Starting from a claim of the angels, the Mashgiach asks what the 'altar of earth' means. As a mezuzah must be affixed to become part of the house, and tzitzis become part of the garment, Rashi teaches that the altar must be attached to the ground; so too Purim was fixed for all generations and became part of the Jewish year.

title.en: Noach's ark and the calculation of the end

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes Noach building the ark for 120 years while people mocked him and the flood did not yet come. He then tells of Achashverosh, who calculated when the seventy years of exile would end and feared the rebuilding of the Beis HaMikdash.

title.en: Mordechai, the 'ish yemini', belongs to Jerusalem

summary.en: Achashverosh makes a great feast to celebrate that the seventy years passed without redemption, and Mordechai goes about declaring that he belongs to Jerusalem: the passuk calls him 'ish yemini', and Binyamin was called 'son of the right' because Eretz Yisrael is called 'yemin'. The Mashgiach says that tonight even a Jew living in Boro Park rejoices that it is Purim in Jerusalem, as in 'Samachti b'omrim li'.

The Mashgiach connects Esther's feast, prepared before Pesach, with clearing out the chametz: Haman's fall was a biur chametz. He explains that reclining at the Seder is the mark of freedom, and that Haman fell onto the couch.

The Mashgiach brings the Satmar Rav's saying that on the Seder night not only the piece of matzah but the whole night is matzah, and explains 'tonight all of us recline'. He returns to Haman falling on the couch and asks that all the enemies of Israel fall like Haman.
Interlude.

title.en: Children of Hashem and Purim tzedakah

summary.en: The Mashgiach says that tonight Jews far away can be brought close to Hashem. He brings Rabbi Akiva's answer that Jews are children of Hashem, and a father wants others to have mercy on his child; this is why Jews have the mitzvah of tzedakah. During the year one may check before giving, but on Purim one gives to everyone, for all are children of Hashem.

title.en: 'Parshas hakesef': the inside of the money

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks what Mordechai's 'parshas hakesef' means and brings Rashi's 'perush hakesef'. The inner meaning of money is 'tocho ratzuf ahavah', the warmth and fire with which a Jew gives; the Beis HaMikdash was built from that, not from cold stones, unlike the towers whose stones can be shattered. Haman could count the half-shekels, but not their fire.

title.en: The milui of kesef is fire

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains 'kesef over lasocher' as currency that is accepted in Heaven, and shows that the filling (milui) of the letters of 'kesef' is 'aish', fire. Avraham bought the Me'aras HaMachpelah and Dovid bought the place of the Beis HaMikdash 'b'kesef malei', with the fullness of kesef: with fire.

The Mashgiach shows that the difference between the numerical values of Yisrael and Amalek is 301, the value of 'aish'. He explains Yaakov's blessing to Binyamin, 'in the morning he devours prey and in the evening divides the spoil', as Shaul's war and the war in the days of Mordechai, both through Binyamin.

title.en: The goral, Yaakov's fire and the wall of fire

summary.en: The Mashgiach compares the lots of Purim with the lots of Yom Kippur, where the two goats must be alike, as Yaakov and Esav appear alike yet Hashem loves Yaakov. The house of Yaakov is fire, which Haman's money could not overcome, and with the matanos la'evyonim given today a wall of fire was built.
Interlude.

The Mashgiach brings the Gemara that Knesses Yisrael complained 'see what the Yehudi did to me', since Dovid did not kill Shimi, from whom Mordechai came, and asks how the Shechinah itself could complain about Mordechai. He recalls what he said before Shabbos Mishpatim about the heichal of guilt and the heichal of merit, and tells the story of the plague in Rav's neighborhood.

title.en: Rav's merit and the Yismach Moshe

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why Rav's great merit did not protect his neighborhood, and brings the Chasam Sofer and the Yismach Moshe, who explains it with a rule of the Rashba about two baskets: only what enters the doubt can combine with the others. A tzaddik so great that the decree does not touch him at all cannot protect others; one who could be included in it can.

title.en: Mordechai brought them into the heichal of merit

summary.en: The Mashgiach applies this to Purim: the Jews of that generation were judged for enjoying the wicked king's feast, and Mordechai, who did not bow, stood with them and pulled them from the heichal of guilt into the heichal of merit; 'mah asah li Yehudi' became the miracle of Purim. He adds the Midrash that Moshe broke the luchos so as to be together with the Jews.
Singing.

title.en: Proofs that the Megillah was said with ruach hakodesh

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara in which the Tannaim prove that Megillas Esther was said with ruach hakodesh, and Shmuel says he has a proof better than all of them, as the saying goes, 'one sharp peppercorn is better than a basket of gourds'.

title.en: Too much fits together to be chance

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that any one detail of the Megillah could be explained by natural reasoning, but all of them together fitting so exactly goes against all statistics and shows a miracle from Heaven. He describes how a man of truth repeats exactly what he heard without adding his own imagination, as Mordechai HaTzaddik did.

The Mashgiach explains that attributing everything to chance comes from the klipah of Amalek. Eliyahu at Har HaCarmel, after fire came down from Heaven, had to pray a second time that the people should not say it was witchcraft; so one must pray to be spared Amalek's coldness.

title.en: Kiymu v'kiblu: a proof from emunah

summary.en: The Mashgiach returns to the Tannaim's proofs, each of which the Gemara could answer, and to Shmuel's 'kiymu v'kiblu', that Heaven upheld above what the Jews accepted below. This proof rests on emunah, and that is why it is better than all the others.
Interlude.

The Mashgiach speaks of 'he brought me to the house of wine' and the wine of Jerusalem, and brings the Gemara that one born under the mazal of Ma'adim will be a shedder of blood. He connects the wine of Purim with Jerusalem and with the wine kept for the future.

title.en: The song of Shabbos and a closing blessing

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that 'mizmor shir l'yom haShabbos' is a song for the future, the day that is entirely Shabbos, and that Jerusalem is Shabbos. He closes with a blessing that all should merit to praise and thank Hashem as is fitting, with great joy.
Closing.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that the Aseres Yemei Teshuvah, the Beis HaMikdash and Adam HaRishon are each the hidden point of origin of time, place and soul, which is why each must be searched for, and why these days call for searching and for creating oneself anew.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Gemara reading 'Dirshu Hashem b'himatzo' as the ten days from Rosh Hashanah to Yom Kippur, and links them to the other thing the Torah says must be searched for, the place of the Beis HaMikdash, which David HaMelech sought without sleep. He explains that the Mikdash is the Even Shesiyah, the point from which the world grew, and that Har, mountain, relates to herayon, conception, while hirhur, thought, is the 'mountain on top of the mountain'. Using the Sefer Yetzirah's triad of olam, shanah and nefesh, he shows that the Mikdash, Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, and Adam HaRishon are the origin points of place, time and soul. An origin is elusive, as Shmuel's search for David, the search for the Mikdash's site and the Levi'im's mistake about Rosh Hashanah show. The Sanhedrin's authority, too, comes from the place where Torah, the blueprint of the world, goes forth. He closes that in these days one creates oneself through the shofar and the pesukim, must not sleep, and must search, as the last generation will search for Hashem.

en: The Mashgiach links two things the Torah says must be searched for: Hashem in the ten days of teshuvah, and the site of the Beis HaMikdash.
The Beis HaMikdash is the Even Shesiyah, the point from which Hashem began forming the world, and so it is called a Har, related to herayon, conception.

Following the Sefer Yetzirah, the world exists as olam, shanah and nefesh, and each has a Kodesh HaKodashim and a point of origin: the Mikdash in place, Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur in time, and Adam HaRishon in soul.
Rosh Hashanah is herayon, the conception of the year, while Yom Kippur is hirhur, the thought that precedes it, 'the mountain on top of the mountain'.
Every point of origin is elusive and needs searching, because it begins in thought and is not yet tangible.
In the Aseres Yemei Teshuvah one creates oneself anew, through the shofar and the ten pesukim of Malchiyos, Zichronos and Shofros, which correspond to the ten utterances of creation.
