title.en: Purim joy and the rav of Amsterdam

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens by saying that Purim is a time when simcha can bring great salvations for Jews. He tells how Rabbi Elazar of Amsterdam, asked to pray when the dams broke, was found dancing and drinking with his students, because on Purim this accomplishes more than tehillim and fasts.

The Mashgiach brings from sefarim that Yaakov Avinu laid the ground for Purim when he prayed to be saved from Esav, words whose initials hint to Haman. With the Chasam Sofer he explains that Yaakov died in Egypt so that his holiness would remain with the Jews outside Eretz Yisrael, and that Yaakov runs through all generations like the middle bar of the Mishkan.

The Mashgiach speaks of the Jews driven further and further into exile, who are not forgotten before Hashem, and brings from the Chernobyler that Moshiach is the aspect of Mordechai. He shows through gematria that the verse of Yaakov's embalming hints to Chanukah and Purim, and ties Shushan Purim to Yaakov and to Shlomo HaMelech.

title.en: Achashveirosh's feast and Shimi ben Gera

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains, with the Yaaros Devash and the Chasam Sofer, that the sin of the Jews was enjoying a feast held because the Beis HaMikdash was not being rebuilt. He explains that Shimi ben Gera cursed the kingdom of Dovid, yet Mordechai was to come from him, and that Dovid's last words to Shlomo concerned Shimi.

title.en: A stumble as the door to the highest level

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings from Rabbi Tzadok HaKohen that when a person stumbles in something, it is a sign from Heaven that he can now reach the highest level in that very thing. The generation of the flood could have merited the Torah had they done teshuvah, and he brings the Gemara that at Matan Torah the nations feared a new flood, until Bilaam told them that Hashem was giving strength, the Torah, to His people.

The Mashgiach says that in Shushan the Jews failed, yet from that failure came the greatest success, the Beis HaMikdash built with Haman's money. He calls his own generation, in the year 2002, a generation of failure, with pursuit of pleasures, weak emunah and machlokes as in Shushan, and says that from this very failure it can merit great success and the third Beis HaMikdash.

title.en: Achashveirosh on the throne of Shlomo

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Midrash and the Targum Sheni that Achashveirosh wanted to sit on the throne of Shlomo HaMelech, and Knesses Yisrael cried, 'Do not disgrace the throne of Your glory.' He explains that the feast imitated the Beis HaMikdash, applies the cry to Yishmael sitting today on the place of the Mikdash, and closes with a tefillah that the merit of Purim bring the rebuilding.
Singing.

The Mashgiach brings the Midrash that the redeemer of parshas Behar is Mordechai and 'his uncle's son' is Esther. He then brings the Midrash that Haman told Mordechai his grandfather Yaakov had bowed to Esav, and explains that Yaakov bowed to the Shechinah that passed before him, not to Esav; Mordechai is called Yehudi because he declares the One G-d.

The Mashgiach explains that Mordechai embodies a lofty level called yesod abba, also called geulah, before which one must stand. He brings the Bnei Yissaschar that had Mordechai bowed it would have caused a blemish in all the worlds, and asks why Mordechai, a gilgul of Yaakov, could not rely on the Shechinah as Yaakov did.

The Mashgiach answers that above the revealed level called 'Atah' there is a hidden world called 'Hu', which will be revealed with Moshiach as 'This is our G-d', the fiftieth gate, and which was revealed at Yetzias Mitzrayim and on Purim. Mordechai wanted the Shechinah revealed openly, so he would not bow and Haman would fall before him; the Rambam brings that Purim will never be nullified.

title.en: Yerushalayim, Esther and the hidden love

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Baal HaTurim that geulah is mentioned nineteen times in parshas Behar, matching the brachos of Shemoneh Esrei, and ties Mordechai and Esther to the brachos of the tzaddikim and of Yerushalayim. With the Pri Tzaddik on 'I have loved you' he explains that though Yaakov and Esav look alike, Hashem alone sees the hidden love in a Jew, the level of not knowing between cursed Haman and blessed Mordechai.

title.en: The Roman king's walls of shoes

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara that Achashveirosh wore the bigdei kehunah, and the piyut of the Ten Martyrs, in which the Roman king covered his walls with shoes to recall the sale of Yosef for shoes. With the Shelah he explains that shoes separate a person from the earth, so the brothers, who would not separate themselves from the holy land, bought shoes once they sinned; every king is moved by his heavenly minister to arouse such accusations, like the shoes hung on wires in the streets today.

title.en: The shoham stones and the world above sin

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Achashveirosh, who feared the Beis HaMikdash, wore the bigdei kehunah so that the tribes' names on the shoham stones would recall the sale of Yosef and the baseless hatred that destroyed it. But he did not know Rashi: the names were engraved in order of birth, before the sin, pointing to a world above sin, like the Kodesh HaKodashim that even an angel may not enter.

title.en: The hidden treasure Haman did not know

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Haman's accusation of a scattered and divided people turned around, since the bigdei kehunah aroused the root of Israel above sin. Haman did not know that Moshe was born on the seventh of Adar, for he has no share in the hidden light; that root is revealed through Shema Yisrael, which Haman feared, and the Mashgiach laments the many Jews today who do not know what Shema Yisrael means.
Singing.

title.en: Esther in the inner court: pure mesiras nefesh

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Zohar's parable of a king who visits his bride in a tannery: so the Shechinah came down to Esther in Achashveirosh's palace. He brings the Gemara's question why Esther invited Haman, and explains her pure mesiras nefesh, like Avraham at the Akeidah, who had everything to lose: she was ready to be remembered in disgrace for all generations, only to save the Jews.

title.en: Esther, Esther: a love no waters can quench

summary.en: The Mashgiach continues that Esther's mesiras nefesh was like Avraham's, and brings the Midrash that she put on royalty 'on the third day' in the merit of Avraham at the Akeidah. As Avraham was called 'Avraham, Avraham' with affection, so was Esther, for her love was one that many waters cannot quench; standing now with Esther in the inner court, he says, is a time to daven.
An interlude.

title.en: Written with ruach hakodesh: Shmuel's proof

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara in Megillah that Megillas Esther was said with ruach hakodesh, and that the greatest Tannaim each brought a proof, while Shmuel said a better one: 'they fulfilled and accepted', above as below. Rava said every proof can be pushed off except Shmuel's, and the Mashgiach explains that prophecy remains with Klal Yisrael as a whole.

title.en: If not prophets, sons of prophets

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Hillel, who did not know how the knives would be brought when Erev Pesach fell on Shabbos and said to see what the Jews do; they placed them in the sheep's wool. He explains that simple Jews who cling to the tzaddikim sense what Hashem wants, that a minhag Yisrael is Torah, that Purim reveals the depth of the Jewish heart, and that the last halachah of hilchos Purim speaks of minhagim.

title.en: Proofs that can be pushed off

summary.en: The Mashgiach says that Haman had no share in the inner point of Israel, and tells of chassidim speaking of a tzaddik's ruach hakodesh in the presence of the Shinever Rav. He then shows how a proof of the Tannaim can be pushed off, with the example of 'Haman said in his heart', and asks whether all the proofs together can be pushed off.

The Mashgiach explains that Shmuel brought something new: not a logical proof and not a derashah, but the plain fact that the Jews accepted the Megillah, and what Jews accept below is agreed above. Whatever Jews do together is with ruach hakodesh, for the Jewish heart senses Hashem's will; prophecy was taken from the individual but never from the community.
An interlude.

title.en: Mordechai the Yehudi: a mitzvah that includes all

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings that whoever denies idolatry is called a Yehudi, and explains that denying idolatry is a mitzvah that includes the whole Torah. Just as every Jew has a letter in the Sefer Torah, every Jew has his own mitzvah; Mordechai's was this all-inclusive one, which made him the tzaddik of the generation, and in the future Moshiach, as a king, will fight that battle.

The Mashgiach explains that Mordechai's mitzvah was 'do not bow to them', which in gematria points to Haman, and that Haman raged when he heard of it. Above it stands 'I am Hashem your G-d', the root and king of all the mitzvos, which corresponds to Moshiach the king; he ends with a gematria linking the Purim joy to the praise of Yerushalayim.
Singing.

title.en: Esther's seven maidens and the Vilna Gaon

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why Esther needed seven maidens to know when Shabbos was, and tells how the Ger Tzedek Graf Potocki asked the Vilna Gaon how a Jew in the desert could fail to sense Shabbos; the Gaon agreed that an elevated Jew senses it, but the Gemara speaks of those who do not. He answers that Achashveirosh's house held such tumah that the Shechinah withdrew, so Esther needed a sign, and Hashem still came to His bride there.

The Mashgiach explains that Esther, who hid who she was, could not show that she kept Shabbos, yet longed to say 'Shabbos' aloud, so she named the seventh maiden Shabbos and called out to her; only Hashem and Esther knew the secret. He then brings the program to a close and turns to the wine.

The Mashgiach explains that the wine of Purim is not ordinary wine but the wine preserved since the six days of Creation, the inner point of every Jew. He brings the Gemara that on the seventh day, Shabbos, Jews sing Hashem's praises over their wine, and that each guest received wine older than himself, which for Mordechai meant wine from Eretz Yisrael from before the churban, sealed in the vessels of the Beis HaMikdash.

title.en: Wine, blood and the four cups

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara that one should not drink red wine, for it belongs to the mazal of Maadim, and explains that yayin equals seventy, the Name Havayah together with dam, so wine drunk with holiness turns into song. The preserved wine of Purim, whose gematria equals Esther, prepares for the four cups of Pesach and brings the fall of Haman.
Singing.
Singing.
Singing.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Shemitah is Yerushalayim in time: in the seventh year the constant Shabbos of Yerushalayim spreads over all of Eretz Yisrael, and every Jew becomes like a Kohen whose portion is Hashem.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Ponevezher Rav greeting Eretz Yisrael with 'Gut Shabbos' on the night Shemitah began, and asks what Shemitah is. Everything exists in place, time and soul; as Yerushalayim is Shabbos in place, Shemitah is Yerushalayim in time. Yerushalayim is always Shabbos and Shemitah: nothing is planted there, it belongs to no tribe, and no one owns it, just as in Shemitah Hashem reminds the farmer that the land is His and its produce is ownerless. Yaakov, the trunk of the tree, is Shabbos, while the twelve tribes are the weekdays, the twelve Roshei Chodashim and the twelve middle brachos of Shemoneh Esrei. In Shemitah every Jew becomes like the Kohanim and Levi'im, who have no field and live from Hashem. Shemitah is not a new kedushah but an extension of Yerushalayim, like adding to Shabbos, which explains Rabbi Akiva's teaching of tosefes shevi'is. Turning to Kislev, he explains that Yishmael's bow is countered by the Jewish 'bow' of tefillah.

en: Everything exists in place, time and soul, and Shemitah is to time what Yerushalayim is to place.
In the Shemitah year Yerushalayim spreads over all of Eretz Yisrael, and the whole land becomes Shabbos.
Shemitah reminds the owner that the land belongs to Hashem; like Yerushalayim, which belongs to no tribe, its produce is ownerless.
Yaakov, the trunk of the tree, is Shabbos; the twelve tribes correspond to the twelve Roshei Chodashim and the weekday requests of Shemoneh Esrei.
In Shemitah every Jew becomes like a Kohen, without a portion of land, free for Torah.
Shemitah is not a new kedushah descending like Shabbos but an extension of Yerushalayim, a tosefes like the addition to Shabbos.
Kislev, whose mazal is the bow, is the time for the Jewish bow of tefillah to overcome the bow of Yishmael.

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how the Ponevezher Rav greeted Eretz Yisrael with 'Gut Shabbos' when a Shemitah year began, then explains that everything exists in place, time and soul, and that Shemitah is in time what Yerushalayim is in place.

title.en: Yerushalayim: always Shabbos, owned by no one

summary.en: He explains that Yerushalayim is a constant Shabbos and Shemitah: no planting is done there, it was not divided among the tribes, and its houses may not be rented to pilgrims. In Shemitah the land rests, Hashem reminds the farmer it is His, and its produce is ownerless.

title.en: Yaakov the trunk and the twelve tribes

summary.en: He brings the Chinuch on the purpose of Shemitah, notes that Torah goes out from Yerushalayim, and describes Klal Yisrael as a tree: Yaakov is the trunk and Shabbos, with a portion without boundaries, while the twelve tribes are the branches, the twelve Roshei Chodashim and the twelve weekday brachos of Shemoneh Esrei.

title.en: In Shemitah every Jew becomes a Kohen

summary.en: He explains that the Kohanim and Levi'im have no portion of land, belong to Yerushalayim and teach Torah, and that in Shemitah every Jew becomes like them. The sixth year prepares for Shemitah like Erev Shabbos, and in the future all Jews will be Kohanim.

title.en: Shemitah as a tosefes of Yerushalayim

summary.en: He explains that Shemitah is not a new kedushah like Shabbos but Yerushalayim spreading out, like adding time to Shabbos. With this he explains Rabbi Akiva's teaching from 'in plowing and harvest you shall rest' that one adds to Shemitah, and concludes that Shabbos has a tosefes just as Shemitah is one.

Turning to the season, he brings the Targum Yonasan that the twelve Nesi'im read on Chanukah stand against the twelve princes of Yishmael, from whom we suffer at the end of the exile. All of Kislev belongs to Chanukah, it is the time to daven about Yishmael, and the Ba'al HaTurim says that when Yishmael's princes fall Moshiach will come.

title.en: The bow of tefillah against Yishmael's bow

summary.en: He asks why the Torah tells that Yishmael became an archer, and answers with Onkelos, who renders Yaakov's 'my bow' as 'my tefillah': the bow of tefillah neutralizes Yishmael's bow, and Kislev, whose mazal is the bow, is the time for it. He mentions Yishmael's hold on Har HaBayis and closes with a call to use the time and a brachah.

oneLiner.en: At the Purim seudah the Mashgiach teaches that Purim was made for the Jews of the deepest exile, the 'tribe of Dan' at the end of the camp, to whom Hashem comes down in the hiding of His Face, and that a new Megillah of hidden miracles is being written in every generation.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with Esther, who went alone to the palace of Achashverosh, the seat of the sitra achra, and found favor there; so too Knesses Yisroel finds favor before Hashem in the deepest exile. From the Gemara's answer that walled cities must read the Megillah because 'they too are Jews', he explains that in exile Jews live on Chanukah and Purim. Purim's miracles are hidden, and a new Megillah is written every day. He speaks of Shushan Purim as the time to tread on Esav, of the wine at Achashverosh's feast, and of Esther's cry in the house of idols: Purim was made for the villagers and the tribe of Dan, and on it Hashem visits the sick of the exile. He ends with Daniel, the fall of Babylon, Yaakov's blessings, the four cups and the Ne'ilah of Purim.

en: Even in the lowest state of exile, like Esther in Achashverosh's palace, Knesses Yisroel finds favor before Hashem, and the lower a Jew is the more favor he finds.
The Jewish people cannot exist without the moadim; in exile, like a patient on life support, they live on Chanukah and Purim.
The miracles of Purim are hidden and understood only at the end; a new Megillah is written every day of the exile.
Purim and the whole Megillah were made for the 'villagers', the tribe of Dan cut off at the end of the camp, who long for the Shechinah.
Purim is Hashem's visit to the sick: He comes down to the Jews who cannot move from the exile, as the King came to Esther in the house of idols.
Wine drunk by Jews for the sake of Heaven brought the salvation of Purim, and it still removes fear and brings bitachon and salvations.
The end of Purim is like Ne'ilah, its highest point, when at the wine one can ask Hashem for all of Klal Yisroel.

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes how Esther went alone to Achashverosh, down to the lowest level, into the palace that was the headquarters of the sitra achra, so far that she needed her maidens to know when Shabbos was. Afterwards she wrote the Megillah with ruach hakodesh, and since an author's soul rests in his sefer, Esther's soul and her great light rest in the Megillah.

title.en: Finding favor in the deepest exile

summary.en: Bringing the Ohr HaChaim that before Moshiach Jews descend to the fiftieth gate of impurity, the Mashgiach explains that as Esther found favor in the palace of idols, Knesses Yisroel finds favor before Hashem in today's exile. Like the tribe of Dan, who traveled last, the lower a Jew is the more favor he finds, and so a Jew should feel proud.
An interlude.

title.en: Walled cities and the moadim as the nation's soul

summary.en: The Mashgiach takes up the Gemara's suggestion that walled cities might not read the Megillah at all, and its reply, 'are they not Jews?'. He brings the Rambam in Sefer HaMitzvos that without semichah the calendar depends on Jews in Eretz Yisroel, who will therefore always be there, since the Jewish people cannot exist without the moadim, which are its soul; and like a sick person, Jews in exile need life support.

title.en: Chanukah and Purim sustain Jews in exile

summary.en: In Eretz Yisroel Jews had Pesach, Shavuos and Sukkos; in exile they need Chanukah and Purim, which the Zohar counts among 'His moadim'. Since Jews are always called children of Hashem, as Rabbi Meir holds, they must have Purim, and this is the Gemara's answer that the walled cities too are Jews.
An interlude.

title.en: A new Megillah is written every day

summary.en: The miracles in Egypt were recognized as they happened, but the hidden miracles of the Megillah were understood only at the end, like pieces of a puzzle. The Mashgiach says that great miracles happened yesterday and today, Purim 5763, and that a new Megillah is now being written; the name Purim, in the plural, and the words 'it was written in the book' point to the many miracles of every day.
An interlude.

title.en: Shushan Purim, the full moon and Esav's border

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Shushan Purim is the beauty of Purim, when the moon is full; Esther is likened to the moon, and after the fifteenth the moon begins to wane, which is why the Rema writes not to make a wedding then. When the moon wanes Esav grows strong: Edom told the Jews 'you shall not pass through me', and Hashem told them not to enter his land 'until the tread of a foot', which Rashi explains as until Moshiach.

When Mordechai mounted the horse he stepped on Haman, answering him with 'you shall tread on their high places', the last words of Moshe Rabbeinu. The Mashgiach explains that Purim is a time when one may tread on Esav, which is why the feet are stamped at the Megillah; Purim is mentioned five times in the Megillah, and Shushan Purim, the last, is the time to tread on Esav.

The Mashgiach contrasts how gentiles drink with how Jews drink, with words of Torah and songs of praise; by one reckoning the seventh day of the feast was the first day of Pesach, and the Jews drank the four cups. Since each guest was served wine older than himself, while Eretz Yisroel lay desolate for fifty-two years after the churban, the wine had to come from before the churban, brought by Nevuchadnetzar, which raises the question of stam yeinam.

title.en: The Chasam Sofer on Yosef's old wine

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Chasam Sofer that Yosef sent Yaakov old wine from before the time of Avraham Avinu, because the family had accepted a prohibition on such wine, and a decree does not take hold of what existed before it, as the Rosh writes on the meat brought into Eretz Yisroel and on gentile cheese and cooking. He asks how wine, forbidden by a later spoiling, compares to cheese and cooking, forbidden by the making itself, but concludes that one cannot argue with the Chasam Sofer.

title.en: Mordechai and Haman on the wine

summary.en: Wine of Eretz Yisroel carries great holiness. Mordechai held that the wine from the time of the first Beis HaMikdash was kosher and wanted Jews to drink it for Hashem's sake, while Haman claimed it was stam yeinam, to make them stumble; the four cups they drank brought nachas ruach above, Vashti's downfall and Esther's rise. The Mashgiach says that wine drunk for the sake of Heaven still removes fear, brings bitachon and songs of praise, and brings salvations.
Singing.

title.en: Esther's cry and the villagers who read early

summary.en: Esther cried 'Keli, Keli, lamah azavtani' when the Shechinah left her in the house of idols, and the Mashgiach asks why she merited ruach hakodesh there, when Moshe Rabbeinu had to leave the city to daven. He brings the Mishnah that villagers read early, on the day of assembly when they come to the courts, and the Gemara that a man who always wanted to go to din was from the tribe of Dan; the whole Purim was made for the children of Dan, the stragglers at the end of the camp, who are like the Jews in exile among the deniers.

title.en: Why the tribe of Dan loves the court

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the children of Dan love going to the court, and brings Rashi that Avraham sat at the entrance of his tent as a sign that Hashem stands in the congregation of judges. Dan, driven out from under the shadow of the Shechinah, longs for it without knowing why, and so seeks the court where the Shechinah is revealed; the whole Megillah and tractate were made for them, which is why Maseches Megillah opens with the villagers.

title.en: Purim as Hashem's visit to the sick

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings from the kisvei that Purim is a bechinah of visiting the sick: as Hashem visited Avraham, He comes down to the Jews who are sick from the exile. Moshe could leave the city, but Esther, ill in the house of idols, could not move, so the King came to her; he reads 'and You are holy, enthroned upon the praises of Israel' by gematria as Megillas Esther.

title.en: Esther's darkness and the light of Shabbos on Purim

summary.en: Esther lived in such darkness that she did not know when Shabbos was, yet she spoke to Hashem constantly, so that saying 'a foe and an enemy' she pointed at Achashverosh and a malach pushed her hand toward Haman. The Mashgiach says there was never such a hiding of the Face, and Jews serve Hashem within it; on Purim Hashem comes to visit them, and as the Avodas Yisroel of the Kozhnitzer Maggid writes, Purim, though a weekday, carries the light of Shabbos.
An interlude.

Daniel alone saw the vision, though Chaggai, Zecharia and Malachi were greater; the Mashgiach explains that Moshiach will come when Jews descend to the lowest levels, the souls of Dan, and Daniel, who went down to that lowest level, could reveal the end of days. He then speaks of the ruler of Iraq, who declared himself the successor of Nevuchadnetzar, king of Babylon, and seeks weapons of destruction against the Jews.

title.en: The fall of Babylon is in the Megillah

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the weapons of Yishmael will not succeed, though the exile of Yishmael is the hardest, as the Rambam writes in Iggeres Teiman. Each generation has its own Megillah; the Sfas Emes says that before Moshiach Hashem will make a miracle like Purim to strengthen the Jews. Since Nevuchadnetzar is named in the Megillah and its first pesichta speaks of cutting off Babylon, the salvation from Babylon already lies in it, and Jews need have no fear.
An interlude.

title.en: The last letters of the Sefer Torah

summary.en: The last lines of a Sefer Torah are written by ordinary Jews at the siyum and are less beautiful; the Mashgiach explains that every soul is a letter, and the Jews of the exile, the souls of Dan, are the last letters, which Yehoshua wrote and which are still part of the Torah. Faded letters are kosher in a Megillah because it is called a letter (iggeres), sent personally to every Jew; the holiness of Israel is a segulah beyond reason.
A niggun.

title.en: Yaakov receives the blessings as Esav

summary.en: Bringing Rabbi Tzadok HaKohen, the Mashgiach explains that Yaakov said 'I am Esav' because he wanted to receive the blessings also for the generations of Jews who look like Esav, even the 'traitors' in 'the scent of his garments'. Every Jew inwardly wants Hashem's will, as the Rambam explains 'they compel him until he says I want'; this inner will comes out on Yom Kippur and Purim, whose lots are one, as the two goats look alike and only Hashem knows which is His. Yaakov's wine, the preserved wine, is by gematria Esther.

The four cups are learned from the four times 'cup' in the dream of the chief butler and from the four expressions of redemption. The Mashgiach explains that the cups hold two kinds of wine: a cup of wrath for the enemies of the Jews, poured out at 'pour out Your wrath upon the nations', and the holy wine of binah that remains. The wine of Achashverosh's feast brought Vashti's downfall; the Yishmaelim do not drink wine, but Jews do.
An interlude.

title.en: Haman's ten sons and the Ne'ilah of Purim

summary.en: The ten sons of Haman are the ten crowns of the sitra achra; when they fell, the kingship of holiness, Moshiach ben David, was revealed, and Vayzasa is by gematria Moshiach ben David. The end of Purim, when Jews gather to drink wine, is like Ne'ilah, its highest point; and as the king asked Esther 'what is your request' at the wine, the Mashgiach says that now one can ask for Klal Yisroel.
An interlude.
The Mashgiach wishes that each Jew find within himself the Jewish neshamah, the point of Yiddishkeit that rejoices before Hashem, together with all Jews.

oneLiner.en: At the Purim seudah the Mashgiach teaches that Purim reaches down to the weakest Jews and the faded letters of the Torah, repairing souls, renewing emunah and the Oral Torah, and revealing the guarded wine and the circular light of Moshiach.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with Jerusalem and Shushan Purim as the root of the Oral Torah that the Jews accepted on Purim, and explains that Purim was made for the weakest, 'weekday' souls. He links the Tannaim gathered in Bnei Brak to Haman's descendants and their difficulty with Krias Shema, tells of the Megillah read on the Seder night, and traces Vashti's spark of Shabbos to the cow of Rabbi Chanina ben Torasa. He describes Purim as a second match with Hashem and a battle over emunah, the faded last letters of the Torah as the weak souls, and Adar as a circle in which the end touches the beginning. In the second part he explains Moshe's last word 'tidroch' as Haman's downfall, why the Jews went to Achashverosh's feast, namely to rescue the Beis HaMikdash's wine, and the guarded wine that equals Esther.

en: Purim was made for the weakest, 'weekday' souls; this is why it was not accepted as a yom tov on which work is forbidden and why the Megillah is read on weekdays.
On Purim the Jews accepted the Oral Torah anew, and Jerusalem, celebrated on Shushan Purim, is the root of the Oral Torah.
The war against Amalek is a war over emunah, and Purim calls for a cheshbon hanefesh about one's emunah.
Purim throws a rope to every Jew, even the one who no longer knows the difference between Haman and Mordechai.
Adar is like a circle in which the end touches the beginning: Moshe died and was born in Adar, and Purim brings down the light of the days of Moshiach.
A person's last word expresses his essence, and Moshe's last word in the Torah, 'tidroch', brought about Haman's downfall.
The Jews went to Achashverosh's feast to rescue the Beis HaMikdash's vessels and its wine for the nesachim and to drink their Seder cups from it, not to celebrate.

candidateTopics: Achashverosh's feast and the Beis HaMikdash wine

title.en: Shushan Purim, Jerusalem and the Oral Torah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that on Purim the Jews accepted the Oral Torah anew, and that Jerusalem, the walled city of Shushan Purim, is its root. He shows that the joy of Jerusalem, not stated outright in the Megillah, is derived through a gezeira shava and is tied to Yehoshua, who first fought Amalek.
Singing.

The Mashgiach notes that the Jews did not accept Purim as a yom tov on which work is forbidden, and explains that there are Shabbos souls, Yom Tov souls and Chol HaMoed souls. Purim was made for the weakest Jews, the weekday souls: the Megillah is read on weekdays, the Jews are called Yehudim, and it parallels the twelve weekday blessings of Shemoneh Esrei that correspond to the Shevatim.

title.en: Haman's descendants in Bnei Brak and Krias Shema

summary.en: Starting from the Haggadah's Tannaim in Bnei Brak who sat until the time of the morning Shema, the Mashgiach connects Jews who struggle with Krias Shema to the Gemara that Haman's descendants learned Torah in Bnei Brak. Zeresh, who wanted Mordechai hanged in the morning to stop Krias Shema, fled to Bnei Brak; her descendants who converted carried a blemish in Krias Shema, and the Tannaim came there to repair it.

title.en: The Megillah on the Seder night

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells a story related by the Spinka Rebbe about a Jew who read the Megillah on the second Seder night so that a soul could receive its tikkun, and says he firmly believes souls come for a tikkun when Jews gather on Purim. He then suggests that the Tannaim in Bnei Brak learned the Megillah on the Seder night to repair the souls of Haman's descendants.

Bringing the Ba'al Shem Tov and a story of the Divrei Chaim, the Mashgiach teaches that where there is no fear, harsh judgments cannot take hold. Zeresh wanted to keep the Jews in fear and away from Krias Shema, the Gemara's remedy for fear, but Mordechai heard a child's verse 'do not fear sudden terror', and in the end the fear of Mordechai fell on the enemies. He concludes that a Jew should say the morning Shema with clarity and accept the yoke of Heaven.

The Mashgiach brings the Midrash about a Jew's cow, sold to a gentile, that would not work on Shabbos until its former owner whispered in its ear; seeing the greatness of the Jews, the gentile converted and became the Tanna Rabbi Chanina ben Torasa. From Gilgulei Neshamos he adds that Achashverosh was reincarnated in that gentile and Vashti in the cow.

title.en: Vashti's spark of Shlomo and Shabbos

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Vashti, a granddaughter of Nevuchadnetzar and through him a descendant of Shlomo HaMelech, the soul of Shabbos, carried a spark of Shabbos that she tried to tear out by making Jewish girls work on Shabbos. Her tikkun came through the cow that was forced to work on Shabbos and through the convert ben Torasa, which he finds in remazim on Mizmor Shir l'Yom HaShabbos and on Dovid HaMelech's chapter for Shlomo.

title.en: Achashverosh's display and the second match

summary.en: Following the Chasam Sofer, the Mashgiach explains that Achashverosh, whose kingdom was not established, wanted to show Vashti as proof that Heaven had given him a worthy wife, and she showed the opposite. On the deeper level the king is Hashem: Purim was a second match and a second Kabbalas HaTorah, like the Second Beis HaMikdash in which the Oral Torah flourished.

title.en: Emunah against Amalek, and 'ad d'lo yada'

summary.en: The Mashgiach teaches that the war against Amalek, whose name equals 'safek' (doubt), is a war over emunah, and that Purim calls for a cheshbon hanefesh about one's emunah. He warns of devices that uproot emunah and purity, and answers how the Gemara can require drinking until one cannot tell Haman from Mordechai: Purim throws a rope even to the lowest Jew, the one who no longer knows the difference.

title.en: The faded last letters of the Torah

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of a gadol who recognized that a beautiful Sefer Torah was written by a heretic because its last letters were perfect, without the custom of leaving them for others to fill in. He traces the custom to the last eight verses that Moshe wrote in tears, and explains that every Jew is a letter in the Torah: the faded last letters are the weak souls who fell from the camp, and Adar and Megillas Esther belong to them.

Citing Rabbi Tzadok and the teaching of igulim and yosher, the Mashgiach explains that in this world Hashem leads with a straight line that has a beginning and an end, while in the days of Moshiach there will be a circle, like the round dance Hashem will make for the tzaddikim, in which all are equal. Purim draws down this circular light of Moshiach and will therefore never be nullified.

title.en: Adar: the end touches the beginning

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Haman rejoiced in Adar, the month of Moshe's death, thinking it was the end of the Jewish people, but did not know that Moshe was also born in Adar: in a circle the end touches the beginning. Esther asked for a 'tomorrow' of Moshiach's light, and Mordechai's appointment in the Beis HaMikdash over the bird-offerings of women after childbirth shows that he oversees the rebirth of Klal Yisrael as a newborn nation.

title.en: Closing: a day to make peace with Hashem

summary.en: Between songs, the Mashgiach recalls that Purim is a day of cheshbon hanefesh on which even one who is 'cursed like Haman' can reconcile with Hashem and begin anew as a newborn nation; then all sing 'Lomir zich iberbeten'.

The Mashgiach explains that the camp of Israel was like a Sefer Torah in which every Jew has his letter and place, and that Yisro found his place by adding a parsha to the Torah. Haman claimed the Jews are 'scattered' and have no place; with the wiping out of Amalek they received their place, the Beis HaMikdash in Jerusalem. He contrasts Eliyahu, the angel of the bris, with Haman, both connected to the mazal of Ma'adim.

title.en: Shushan Purim paves the roads to Jerusalem

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that every sin is a kind of murder and that the sword belongs to the mazal of Ma'adim, while Eliyahu, remembered in Charvona 'zachur latov', turns it to good. The fall of Haman's house is the building of Jerusalem, and Shushan Purim prepares the roads to the city of refuge so that every Jew can reach his place in Jerusalem; he closes with a heartfelt plea to Hashem to build Jerusalem.
Singing.

title.en: A person's last word, and Moshe's last word

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that a person's last word expresses his whole essence, bringing Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, Rabbi Akiva's 'echad' and Rabba bar Nachmani's 'tahor'. Moshe's last word in the Torah was 'tidroch'; Haman rejoiced over Moshe's death in Adar, but when Mordechai stepped on him to mount the horse and answered him with this verse, Moshe's last word became Haman's downfall.

In honor of the wine, the Mashgiach brings the Gemara that the seventh day, 'when the king's heart was merry with wine', was Shabbos, when the Jews drank wine and sang praises while Achashverosh and his gentiles engaged in frivolity, and then Vashti's fate was sealed. He asks why the long months of feasting did not arouse judgment earlier, and brings the Yalkut and Midrash on the golden cups and the food of Eretz Yisrael, asking what these details teach.

title.en: Why did the Jews go to the feast?

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's teaching that the Jews deserved destruction for enjoying Achashverosh's feast, a feast held to celebrate that the Beis HaMikdash would not be rebuilt. He sharpens the question: Mordechai always showed mesiras nefesh, yet according to the Gemara he was at the feast, and it is unthinkable that Jews went to celebrate the end of their hope; he notes too that old wine from Eretz Yisrael must have been served there.

The Mashgiach answers that among the Temple vessels Achashverosh brought out were sealed vessels of wine prepared for the nesachim. Pained by the desecration, the Jews went to keep the vessels and the wine out of gentile hands and, since according to Rabbi Yonasan Eybeschutz that night was the Seder, to drink their four cups from the Beis HaMikdash's wine and sing Hallel over it. Hashem, the King, was pleased with this wine, and Vashti's punishment followed.

The Mashgiach explains the four cups learned from the four expressions of redemption and from the four cups of Pharaoh: the wine spilled at the plagues is the 'cup of poison' for the nations, while what remains is pure. With the Chasam Sofer he explains why the plagues may be listed in order on the Seder night, and tells how the Sfas Emes accepted the Rebbe of Alexander after hearing him speak of 'yayin hameshumar', the last thing the Chiddushei HaRim had revealed to him.

From the Manos HaLevi's remez that 'vekeilim mikeilim shonim veyayin malchus rav' spells 'meshumar', the Mashgiach explains that the guarded wine of the World to Come is revealed on Purim; 'yayin hameshumar' equals Esther, and this is why Purim's mitzvah is with wine. The Jews' Seder-night wine poured the dregs onto Vashti while they kept the pure wine of binah, and he calls on all to drink and sing to Hashem.
L'chaim and singing.

Between songs, the Mashgiach remarks that after all the stages of Chad Gadya Hashem remains with His kid, mentions the custom of Polish tzaddikim to say Nishmas on Purim night, and describes midnight on Shushan Purim in Jerusalem, which has an aspect of Shabbos, when the angels sing together with the Jews there.
Singing.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Purim, and above all a Purim Meshulash in Yerushalayim, stands above time and place and reveals Hashem's love for every Jew, from its roots in Yosef and Binyamin to the repair of the flaws that brought it about.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach explains that Purim, and above all a Purim Meshulash, stands above time and place. He shows how Rav Shmuel bar Shilas, a descendant of Haman, repaired through faithful teaching the flaw of Yoav's melamed, and rebukes those who scorn teaching children. He tells of Rabbi Yochanan ben Torta's cow, a gilgul of Vashti, and how the despair of the geulah at Achashverosh's feast was repaired. He shows that Binyamin came to Yosef on Purim, making the first Purim Meshulash, and that Chanukah and Purim sustain the Jews in galus. Esther's feast follows Yaakov's counsel of food filled with the zemiros of Shabbos. Purim was made for the forgotten Jews, cannot fall on Shabbos before Moshiach except in Yerushalayim, and, born of sins, reveals Hashem's love from the world of keser.

en: Purim is not bound to time or place, and a Purim Meshulash in Yerushalayim reveals this most of all.
Rav Shmuel bar Shilas, descended from Haman, repaired through faithful teaching the flaw of Yoav's melamed, and from him came 'mishenichnas Adar marbin b'simcha'.
Binyamin came to Yosef on Purim, which fell on Friday, making a Purim Meshulash, and only then could Yaakov go down into galus, since Chanukah and Purim strengthen the Jews there.
Esther learned from her father's house, Binyamin's family, Yaakov's counsel of sending food filled with the zemiros of Shabbos to an enemy, which brings about his downfall.
Purim was made for the forgotten Jews whom Haman thought Hashem had forgotten, and therefore the villagers are the first to read the Megillah.
Before Moshiach the fourteenth of Adar cannot fall on Shabbos, because Esav's boundary still holds; only in walled Yerushalayim can Shushan Purim fall on Shabbos.
Purim came about through sins, and so it reveals that Hashem loves the Jews even when they sin, from the world of keser that no sin reaches.

title.en: Purim Meshulash, above time and place

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens with Rav Aharon of Karlin's words that at Neilah one gate stays closed and opens only on Purim, and calls Purim Meshulash a time to repair souls. He shows from the first Mishnah of Megillah that Purim is not bound to one day or place, and speaks of the merit of Jews who come from abroad to keep Purim in Yerushalayim.
An interlude.

title.en: Rav Shmuel bar Shilas and Haman's generosity

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks how a rasha like Haman had the generosity to offer ten thousand talents of silver, and answers that it was the spark of his descendant Rav Shmuel bar Shilas, the devoted melamed. Through the Gemara of Yoav and his teacher he shows that Rav Shmuel bar Shilas came into being through that teacher's mistake, and that his faithful teaching repaired it.

title.en: Terumas hadeshen and the calling of a melamed

summary.en: From the kohen's garment that must fit him and the Mishnah in Yoma about the lottery for terumas hadeshen, the Mashgiach rebukes young men who say teaching children does not suit them: one serves the Ribono shel Olam, and each person's livelihood matches the repair of his soul. He ends with Mordechai, who merited Purim by caring for the children, and a blessing for our children.
Singing.

title.en: Rabbi Yochanan ben Torta and the cow

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of a Jew whose cow, sold to a gentile, would not work on Shabbos until its former owner whispered in its ear; the gentile converted and was called Yochanan ben Torta. He brings that the gentile was a gilgul of Achashverosh and the cow a gilgul of Vashti, who had made Jewish girls work on Shabbos.

title.en: Vashti's feast and faith in Moshiach

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Rabbi Yochanan ben Torta's words to Rabbi Akiva that Bar Koziba was not Moshiach, and explains the sin of Achashverosh's time: Jews joined a feast celebrating that the Beis HaMikdash would not be rebuilt, and Vashti made her own feast to persuade Jewish women that Moshiach would not come. Through the cow and the convert, he says, Vashti and Achashverosh repaired this, for Rabbi Yochanan ben Torta kept the Jews' faith in Moshiach.
Singing.

title.en: Torah doubled in Eretz Yisrael; Yosef and Binyamin in Adar

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara that a Jew from abroad who comes to Eretz Yisrael becomes twice as great, and the Chasam Sofer's words about his Torah, explaining that a Jew and his share in the Torah are one. He then brings Rav Tzadok HaKohen that the geulah needs two tzaddikim, Yosef and Binyamin, which is why Yosef demanded Binyamin before saying 'Ani Yosef', and that it seems to Rav Tzadok this meeting took place in Adar.

title.en: Binyamin came on Purim, the goblet on Shushan Purim

summary.en: The Mashgiach adds that if it was Adar it was Purim: Binyamin's arrival and the meal of 'vayishtu vayishkeru' were on Purim, the brothers seated apart hint to two separate Purims with mishloach manos between them, and the next day, with the goblet, was Shushan Purim, when the moon is full. He links this to Esther's request for a second day, the angel that turned her finger toward Haman, and Yosef's gifts to Binyamin.

title.en: A Purim Meshulash in Yosef's time

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows from 'utvoach tevach vehachen' that Binyamin came on Friday, so Purim was on Friday and Shushan Purim on Shabbos, a Purim Meshulash. With Purim already in place, Yosef could call Yaakov down to Egypt, for, as the Chiddushei HaRim says, Chanukah and Purim strengthen the Jews in galus.

title.en: Yaakov's imprint in Egypt and Yerushalayim's Purim

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Chasam Sofer that Yaakov's passing in Egypt left a lasting imprint there, and reads 'vayachantu harofim es Yisrael' as the heavenly healers preserving Yaakov through Chanukah and Purim. He concludes that Yerushalayim's certain walled-city Purim binds all Jews in galus to Yerushalayim and to the Third Beis HaMikdash.
Singing.
Singing.

title.en: Esther's invitation: learned from her father's house

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why Rabbi Yehoshua, who brings a passuk for Esther's inviting Haman, adds that she learned it from her father's house. He explains that Yaakov sent 'mizimras ha'aretz', food filled with the zemiros of Shabbos, to the lord of Egypt, and as the Kedushas Levi says of Esther's feast, such holy food pulls a rasha out of his impurity and brings his downfall; Binyamin's family kept this counsel and Esther used it.

title.en: Yosef eats from his father's table

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Yosef, who for twenty-two years had not eaten from his father's food, drank with his brothers from Yaakov's shirayim, and this began the Purim seudah. He ties the Purim seudah to 'nachalas Yaakov' and to Shabbos, and brings Zeresh's words to Haman.
Singing.

title.en: The moon's lack and the forgotten Jews

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the lunar year falls short of the solar year and Adar Sheni restores the lost days, and that the stragglers whom Amalek attacked are like the end of the year. He speaks of the shekalim Moshe forgot: Haman thought Hashem had forgotten the forgotten Jews, but Purim was made for them, and the villagers read the Megillah first.
Singing.

title.en: Esav's boundary and why Purim avoids Shabbos

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that until Moshiach Esav's boundary cannot be crossed, as Edom said 'lo sa'avor bi', and that this is the time of the waning moon, so weddings are not made in the second half of the month. For the same reason the fourteenth of Adar cannot fall on Shabbos: Purim is not yet ready to unite with Shabbos, the moon's completeness.

title.en: A weekday festival, and Shabbos in Yerushalayim

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara that Purim's status as yom tov was not accepted and that Rebbi wished to uproot Tisha B'Av, explaining that the world was not yet ready. In walled Yerushalayim, though, Shushan Purim can fall on Shabbos, a glimpse of the time of Moshiach, when the Megillah will be read on Shabbos.

title.en: Simple Jews, the crown of malchus and the full moon

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the simple Jews are the true Jews, and a small act of avodah today is as precious as the mesiras nefesh of earlier generations. On 'vayasem keser malchus b'roshah' he speaks of the moon becoming equal to the sun, counts the five times 'Purim' appears in the Megillah, and blesses that a chuppah be set up in Yerushalayim.

title.en: Three days of kiymu v'kiblu through Shabbos

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Purim is accepting the Torah with love, and that a Purim Meshulash gives three days of 'kiymu v'kiblu', earned by keeping Shabbos. He notes that Erev Pesach also falls on Shabbos this year, and that Amalek, who hates Shabbos, cannot bear it.
Singing.

title.en: Knesses Yisrael's complaint and the world of keser

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara in which Yehuda and Binyamin each claim credit for Purim, and Knesses Yisrael complains of what came from David sparing Shimi and Shaul sparing Agag. He asks how Knesses Yisrael can complain about Purim, and begins to explain the world of keser, the root of every Jew, which no sin reaches.

title.en: Purim born of sins reveals Hashem's love

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Purim came from two sins, David's and Shaul's, and therefore reveals how Hashem loves His people even when they sin, turning it into salvation. He brings the Ba'al HaTanya that Hashem's name is absent from the Megillah because Purim's root is above the names, the Zohar's parable of the king who goes into a foul place for his bride, and the Chasam Sofer that the miracle began just when the Jews sinned.
An interlude.

The Mashgiach tells of the Ropshitzer Rav, who became drunk twice a year without wine, and says that in Yerushalayim one should become drunk from Yerushalayim itself, which earlier generations longed to reach. Since we are simple people we drink wine, but Purim's wine is unlike other wine, as an esrog is worth far more on Sukkos; he asks that every Jew be poured a cup.
Singing.

oneLiner.en: Reading the Alter Rebbe's letter 'Lehaskil HaBinah' alongside Tanya chapter 26, the Mashgiach shows how a Jew who believes that everything comes from Hashem is not moved by suffering, and how sadness over aveiros belongs only at fixed times, never in the middle of learning, davening or business.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens in Tanya chapter 26 and brings the eleventh letter of Igeres HaKodesh, 'Lehaskil HaBinah', to show what the Alter Rebbe demanded of his chassidim: to have no desire for children, life or sustenance beyond what Hashem gives, since a person is recreated from nothing at every moment and nothing bad comes from above. The Mashgiach admits that he himself cannot live this way, and tells of a Lubavitcher mashpia who steadied himself on the way to his daughter's levayah with the letter's opening words. He explains why the letter begins with Binah: the gevuros are sweetened at their root in Binah, and he connects this with the fifty gates of Binah, Pharaoh, and Sefirah. Returning to the Tanya, he teaches that sadness over aveiros during learning, davening or business comes from the yetzer hara, and that remorse belongs at set times. He closes on how Torah brings down the light of any Yom Tov at any time.

en: In 'Lehaskil HaBinah' the Alter Rebbe asks his chassidim not to desire children, life or sustenance beyond what Hashem decides for them, since a person lives 'against his will'.
Since a person is recreated from nothing at every moment and no evil comes down from above, everything is good, only too great a light for us to grasp.
When a person truly has this emunah, the bad is sublimated and becomes good even in its visible form.
Sadness over aveiros that comes during learning, davening or business is from the yetzer hara, which wants to push a person into desires.
Remorse over aveiros is 'by appointment only': before going to sleep, on Erev Shabbos, Erev Rosh Chodesh and Erev Rosh Hashanah, followed by simchah in Hashem's forgiveness.
Torah is above time, so by learning about a Yom Tov a person draws down its light at any time of year.

candidateTopics: times for teshuvah and cheshbon hanefesh

summary.en: The Mashgiach picks up in Tanya chapter 26 and brings Igeres HaKodesh letter 11 to show what was demanded of chassidim two hundred years ago. He reads that a chassid should not desire children, life or sustenance, and should accept whatever life Hashem gives him.

title.en: Recreated every moment, everything is good

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the letter: a person is recreated from nothing every moment, nothing bad comes from above, so he should always be happy. One who feels that he lacks something loves himself and wants to leave Hashem's hand, while one with true emunah sees the bad turn into good.

title.en: Beyond our level; a mashpia at a levayah

summary.en: The Mashgiach says he personally cannot live with such equanimity, and that he read the letter only to show what the chassidim then understood. He tells of a Lubavitcher mashpia who, walking to his daughter's levayah, shook himself with the letter's opening words 'Lehaskil HaBinah', and explains that the letter opens with Binah because the root of the chasadim is there.

title.en: Sweetening gevuros in Binah; Pharaoh and the fifty gates

summary.en: Repeating a Shabbos talk, the Mashgiach explains that gevurah stands directly under Binah ('Ani Binah li gevurah'), so harsh judgments can be sweetened by raising them to their root. He connects this with the fifty gates of Binah at Yetzias Mitzrayim, with Pharaoh who saw blood but not that it would become the blood of milah, and with the fiftieth day of Sefirah.

title.en: Sadness during learning and business is from the yetzer

summary.en: Back in Tanya chapter 26, the Mashgiach explains that one must serve Hashem with joy while learning or davening, and that even a businessman who suddenly feels sorrow over his aveiros in the middle of his work should know it is a trick of the yetzer hara. The yetzer wants him sad so that he will seek relief in desires such as overeating.

title.en: Remorse by appointment; the stain on the coat

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that remorse over aveiros belongs at fixed times named in the Tanya: before sleep, Erev Shabbos, Erev Rosh Chodesh and Erev Rosh Hashanah, after which a person should believe Hashem has forgiven him and rejoice. He gives a mashal of a stain on a coat that matters more the higher the audience, and notes that one without a program has no appointments at all.

title.en: Torah above time; the Sukkah on Shemini Atzeres

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that every time can hold every Yom Tov, since learning Torah, which is above time, draws down the light of Pesach, Yom Kippur or Sukkos at any time. He brings the Mishnah that one who did not eat in the sukkah the first night makes it up on Shemini Atzeres, explained in a Chassidish way as the sukkah escorting us into the house, and compares the Gemara to hidden streams that surface here and there.

oneLiner.en: At the Purim seudah the Mashgiach explains how Purim and the Megillah reach beyond time, place and the ordinary levels of Tanach, giving Jews strength and refuge throughout the galus.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Mishnah that Purim is not bound to one day or place, so the main seudah is at night, rejoicing with Yerushalayim. Yerushalayim's Purim comes only from Torah shebe'al peh, the hidden kallah. Yosef's five garments for Binyamin hint that Binyamin bowed only to a disguised brother, which gave Mordechai his answer to Haman. He discusses Esther's request to write the Megillah, the closing of the 24 books and of prophecy, and why the Megillah is Kesuvim all year but on Purim an igeres of prophecy, like an esrog on Sukkos. In the second part he explains Knesses Yisrael's complaint against Dovid and Mordechai as removing a kitrug, Purim as a city of refuge in time, Esther's mitzvah of returning lost souls, and her holiness before Achashverosh, and closes with wine and blessings.

en: Purim breaks the bounds of time and place, and the main seudah is held at night to rejoice together with Yerushalayim.
The Chachamim could not add a fourth level to Torah, Nevi'im and Kesuvim, so the Megillah closed the 24 books and the era of prophecy.
The Megillah is written for the galus: every nation that attacks the Jews passes away, and Hashem remains with Klal Yisrael.
Knesses Yisrael's complaint against Dovid and Mordechai, and the Sanhedrin's parting from Mordechai, served to remove a kitrug from them.
Purim is a city of refuge in time: every moment of the Purim seudah is a refuge from the yetzer hara.
Esther remained in holiness, and Achashverosh's speaking only through a translator was part of the miracle that kept this hidden.
The wine of Purim carries a holiness that brings out the hidden good in every Jew.

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens with the first Mishnah of Megillah: Purim is not bound to one day or one place. He explains that the main seudah is held at night to rejoice together with Yerushalayim, as a tikkun for Achashverosh's feast, which celebrated that Yerushalayim would not be rebuilt.

title.en: Yerushalayim's Purim and the hidden Oral Torah

summary.en: He notes that the Megillah never says when Yerushalayim keeps Purim; it emerges only from the Gemara's discussion, from Torah shebe'al peh. Through a question he once asked his talmidim about the brachos in Ki Savo, he connects the Oral Torah with Yerushalayim as the kallah, and with Esther, Dovid HaMelech and Moshiach, whose greatness is concealed.

He brings the Gemara that Yosef gave Binyamin five changes of clothing as a hint to Mordechai, and asks how Yosef, raised above the brothers as the shepherd of Israel, could favor one brother, and how Mordechai could wear royal garments of techeles together with linen, which would be shaatnez.

title.en: Did Binyamin bow to a gentile?

summary.en: He brings the Chasam Sofer that Yaakov was pained that Binyamin had bowed to a gentile ruler, and the Midrash in which Haman taunts Mordechai that Yaakov bowed to Esav and Mordechai answers that Binyamin was not yet born. With the Zohar he explains that Yaakov in truth bowed to the Shechinah.

He concludes that had Binyamin bowed to a gentile, Mordechai would have had no answer for Haman; Yaakov's joy at 'ki hu moshel' was that Purim was secured. He then explains that Mordechai wore the royal garments only as a disguise, and that this is what Yosef hinted: Binyamin bowed to a disguised brother, and from disguise came Purim.

title.en: Esther's request: write me for generations

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara that Esther asked the Chachamim to establish the Megillah for generations, and Rashi that she wanted a name. He brings the passuk 'halo kasavti lecha shalishim', which the Gemara reads as limiting Amalek to three mentions, while Rashi on Mishlei reads it as Torah, Nevi'im and Kesuvim, and asks how the two fit.

title.en: The end of an era and the 24 books

summary.en: He explains that at the time of the Megillah the era of the Nevi'im ended and the Anshei Knesses HaGedolah began, and with Esther the 24 books of Tanach were closed. He asks why Nechemia was not given a book under his name while Esther was, and answers that the Chachamim could not add a fourth level beyond Torah, Nevi'im and Kesuvim, so only one could be chosen.

He brings the Chasam Sofer and others on the greatness of the Megillah, and explains that Esther wanted it written for Hashem's name: to show Jews that Hashem is with them even in hester panim. The Megillah reveals G-dliness within hiddenness, like the level of keser.
Interlude.

The Mashgiach explains that Esther wanted to strengthen Klal Yisrael for all generations, knowing that through the Megillah each generation would have its salvations despite its Hamans. He reads 'im al hamelech tov yinasen gam machar' as a prayer that the Megillah last to the end of days, and brings the Rambam that it will remain even when the books of the Nevi'im are nullified.

He asks why Esther is counted among the seven prophetesses while her Megillah stands in Kesuvim. He answers with a mashal: the Department of Agriculture calls an esrog a citrus fruit worth a quarter, yet on Sukkos a Jew pays hundreds of dollars for it, because holy names rest on it only in its time.

title.en: The Megillah becomes an igeres on Purim

summary.en: Applying the mashal, he explains that all year the Megillah is a sefer in Kesuvim, but on Purim it becomes an igeres on the level of Nevi'im; igeres has the letters of esrog. He adds that Esther completed the 24 books and closed the era of prophecy, and brings the Satmar Rav's rule that the last of an era is the greatest.

title.en: A second Purim in a leap year

summary.en: He brings the Maharal that the first Purim was followed by an intercalated month and a second Purim, and that Esther's two feasts hint at this. Since Mordechai is an aspect of Moshiach, he playfully announces that when Moshiach comes there may be another Purim, and reads 'vedover shalom' as Mordechai greeting the Jews on returning.
Singing.

He asks why the Megillah opens with the downfall of Vashti, Nevuchadnetzar's granddaughter, and explains that the Megillah is written for the galus: even in hiddenness Hashem is with the Jews. He illustrates with Chad Gadya, in which every power that attacks the kid is destroyed by the next, while Hashem remains with Klal Yisrael.

title.en: The nations pass, the Jews remain

summary.en: He says the survival of the Jews in galus is a greater miracle than the splitting of the sea, and from 'vahasheivosa el levavecha' describes how Bavel, Rome and the ancient Britons vanished. The Megillah begins as Bavel ends; Jews need not fear the galus, as the Jews who went dancing to the gas chambers declared.

After closing the theme that all nations will pass and the Jews remain, the Mashgiach brings the Gemara on 'ish Yehudi... ish Yemini': Yehudah and Binyamin each claimed credit, while Knesses Yisrael complained against Dovid for sparing Shimi and against Shaul for sparing Agag. He explains Knesses Yisrael as the Shechinah, asks why it complained, and why part of the Sanhedrin parted from Mordechai.

He tells two stories about the machlokes of the Divrei Chaim of Sanz with the Ruzhin family, and explains that the Ruzhin tzaddikim served Hashem on so lofty a level that it aroused a kitrug in Heaven, and the machlokes removed it.

He applies this to Mordechai, who took on a great madreigah and risked himself against Haman. He brings that Rivka came down among kelipos, and the Chasam Sofer that when one becomes a leader people speak against him for his good. Knesses Yisrael's complaint and the Sanhedrin's parting were meant to remove the kitrug from Dovid and Mordechai.

title.en: Moshiach's mitzvah: the cities of refuge

summary.en: He explains that every Jew has his own mitzvah, and Moshiach's mitzvah is the cities of refuge: the three extra cities of 'veyasafta lecha od shalosh arim' were never set aside, which shows that Moshiach will come. Moshe began the mitzvah of arei miklat and Moshiach will complete it.

title.en: Purim, a city of refuge in time

summary.en: Mordechai is a gilgul of Moshe, and what exists in space also exists in time: Purim is an ir miklat in time. Every aveirah kills time, and the yetzer hara chases a person like the avenger of blood; every moment, bite and drink of the Purim seudah is a refuge. He calls not to fear and to flee to Purim, with its bitachon and hope.
Singing.

title.en: Esther's wine and the captive souls

summary.en: He brings the Gemara that the Shechinah left Esther when she called Achashverosh a dog, and asks what was wrong, since he was one. He explains that Esther's mitzvah is hashavas aveidah, returning what is lost, and that at her wine feast two captive souls were present: in Achashverosh, the future Rabbi Yochanan ben Torsa, and in Haman, his descendants who taught Torah. The wine she served began to free them.

He explains that a dog has no spark of holiness, while a lion has a root in the Merkavah. Calling Achashverosh a dog would have cut off the soul within him, so Esther then called him a lion. He ends that one should not call anyone a dog, and that the wine of Purim brings out the good hidden in every Jew.

He brings the Gemara that Achashverosh spoke to Esther only through a translator until she revealed her lineage, and asks how this belongs to the miracle. He explains that Esther stayed pure by sending a shed in her place, while a tzaddik always has Hashem's name on his lips, as Yitzchak sensed with Yaakov; had Achashverosh spoken to her directly, he would have noticed the difference.

The Mashgiach has the wine distributed, saying that Mordechai and Esther come to every Purim seudah and Esther pours the wine, which brings out each Jew's longing to cleave to Hashem. He tells of three waters mixed into the wine, including water blessed by the Baba Sali and water from a spring the Ba'al Shem Tov brought forth, and gives blessings with l'chaim.
Interlude.
He says that on Purim one can accomplish what even Yom Kippur cannot, and wishes that everyone be turned to the good in Torah, tefillah and good middos. Singing follows.
The end of the seudah.

oneLiner.en: At the Purim seudah the Mashgiach teaches that Purim, the Holy of Holies of the year, reaches above reason, and that Esther's feast, a Pesach seder, freed holy sparks hidden even in Haman, Sisera and Achashverosh.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with Hashem's love for Jews, which, like the lot, is above reason, and calls Purim the Holy of Holies of the year, when every Jew can enter and begin anew. He explains why the Gemara gives Rabbi Masna no 'opening' to the Megillah: in the last, hardest pangs of the exile of Yishmael, Hashem opens without a key. Purim belongs above all to simple Jews and to our low generation, and draws its strength from Shabbos. At length he shows that Esther's feast was a Pesach seder that freed holy sparks: Rabbi Akiva from Sisera, Rav Shmuel bar Shilas from Haman, and Achashverosh himself, who returned as Rabbi Yehudah ben Torta and converted through Shabbos. He explains Esther's rule over 127 provinces as the full stature of kedushah, warns against fear, and closes with blessings for Pesach in Yerushalayim.

en: Hashem's love for every Jew is unconditional and above reason, like the lot of Yom Kippur and of Purim, because in every Jew there is a point untouched by sin.
Purim is the Holy of Holies of the year: on Yom Kippur only the Kohen Gadol entered, but on Purim every Jew can, and he should build his year on it and begin a new page.
In the last, hardest pangs of exile there is no strength left to bring the redemption, so Hashem in His mercy will open it without demanding a key.
Purim belongs above all to the simple and low Jews, and our low generation is more connected to Purim than earlier generations.
Esther's feast was a Pesach seder, and through it holy sparks captive in Haman and Sisera were freed and became Rav Shmuel bar Shilas and Rabbi Akiva.
Purim reaches the hidden world of 'lo yada', beyond time, the hidden light and hidden wine that will be revealed with Moshiach.
Esther's rule over 127 provinces is the full stature of kedushah: Keser as the hundreds, Chochmah and Binah as the tens, and the seven middos as the ones.
